board_events.text: Transition metals: filling the inner $(n-1)d$
New electrons enter the penultimate shell — the $(n-1)d$ orbitals, not the outer $ns$.
Four rows result: the $3d$, $4d$, $5d$ and $6d$ series, each starting in Group three.

board_events.text: A metal keeps a hidden inner d 'drawer' below its outer $ns$ pocket — more ways to give change.
IUPAC test: an incomplete $d$-subshell in the atom OR in a common ion.
That partly filled, accessible drawer is the root of every d-block property.

segments.text: <curious>So why do we call the middle block the transition elements?</curious> Picture the periodic table as a long train: the pushy s-block crowds the left doors, the fussy p-block sits on the right, and the steady d-block fills the wide middle berths, bridging the two.

Here is what makes them special. Their newest electrons do not go into the outermost shell; they slip into the penultimate, second-to-last level, the n minus one d orbitals sitting just below the surface.
Do that across the table and you get four horizontal rows, the three d, four d, five d and six d series, and every one of them begins in Group three.
The picture on the board shows it plainly: the transition metals are literally wedged between the reactive s-block on the left and the choosy p-block on the right.

Think of a shopkeeper with coins in his pocket, the outer n s electrons, plus a little cash drawer behind the counter, the inner n minus one d electrons. He can dip into both in many combinations, which is exactly why these metals show variable oxidation states.
So the general configuration is n minus one d, one to ten electrons, over n s, zero, one or two electrons.
That gives us the formal I U P A C definition: a transition element has an incomplete d-subshell either in its neutral atom or in one of its common ions. The inner drawer must be partly open.
Hold on to that one idea. <whisper>Every superpower of these metals traces back to those partly filled, energetically accessible d-orbitals.</whisper>

<curious>तो हम बीच के block को transition elements क्यों कहते हैं?</curious> Periodic table को एक train समझो: बाईं तरफ pushy s-block, दाईं तरफ choosy p-block, और बीच में steady d-block दोनों को bridge करता है।
खास बात ये है: इनके नए electrons outermost shell में नहीं जाते, वो penultimate यानी second-to-last level में जाते हैं — the n minus one d orbitals, surface के just नीचे।
पूरी table में ऐसा करने पर चार rows बनती हैं, the three d, four d, five d और six d series, और हर एक Group three से शुरू होती है।
Board पर साफ दिख रहा है: transition metals बाईं reactive s-block और दाईं choosy p-block के बीच में wedged हैं।

एक shopkeeper सोचो जिसके pocket में coins हैं, यानी outer n s electrons, और counter के पीछे एक cash drawer, यानी inner n minus one d electrons। वो दोनों में से change दे सकता है — इसीलिए variable oxidation states दिखते हैं।
तो general configuration है n minus one d, one to ten electrons, over n s, zero, one या two electrons।
इससे formal I U P A C definition मिलती है: transition element वो है जिसका d-subshell incomplete हो, या तो neutral atom में या किसी common ion में। Inner drawer थोड़ा खुला होना चाहिए।
इस एक idea को पकड़ो। <whisper>इन metals का हर superpower उन्हीं partly filled, accessible d-orbitals से आता है।</whisper>

sections.title: When 'transition' fails: Zn, Cd and Hg

board_events.text: Group 12: the locked-drawer exceptions
Zn, Cd and Hg sit in the d-block but are NOT true transition metals.

board_events.text: Their $d^{10}$ is full in both the atom and the usual $+2$ ion — the drawer is locked shut.
No partly filled d → white/colourless, diamagnetic, only $+2$, poor catalysts.
Caveat one: heavier $4d$ and $5d$ members FAVOUR higher oxidation states — opposite of the p-block inert pair.
Caveat two: 'reactive' is relative — copper is comparatively noble and resists dilute acids.

segments.text: Now a warning that examiners love. Three elements live in the d-block but flunk the transition test: zinc, cadmium and mercury, all in Group twelve.
The reason is their inner drawer. It is permanently locked shut, because they carry a completely filled d-ten configuration.
Look at the two drawers on the board. Manganese keeps its d-drawer partly open, so it is coloured and magnetic; the Group twelve trio keeps theirs sealed.
Crucially, that d-ten is full both in the neutral atom and in the everyday plus two ion. There is simply no partly filled d-subshell to work with.
So they cannot do the d-block tricks. Their common compounds are white or colourless, they are diamagnetic, they show a single fixed plus two state, and they are poor catalysts.

Two more cautions before we trust any trend. First, the heavier four d and five d members actually favour higher oxidation states, the exact opposite of the inert-pair behaviour you met in the p-block.
Second, reactive is relative. Most first-series metals dissolve in mineral acids, but copper is comparatively noble and refuses to, a point we will meet again in the electrode potentials.
अब एक warning जो examiners को बहुत पसंद है। तीन elements d-block में रहते हैं पर transition test में fail होते हैं: zinc, cadmium और mercury, सब Group twelve में।
वजह है इनका inner drawer। वो हमेशा के लिए locked है, क्योंकि इनमें completely filled d-ten configuration होती है।
Board पर दोनों drawers देखो। Manganese का d-drawer partly open है, इसलिए वो coloured और magnetic है; Group twelve वाले sealed रहते हैं।
Important बात: ये d-ten neutral atom में भी full है और रोज़ के plus two ion में भी। कोई partly filled d-subshell बचता ही नहीं।
तो ये d-block tricks नहीं कर पाते। इनके common compounds white या colourless होते हैं, ये diamagnetic हैं, single fixed plus two state दिखाते हैं, और poor catalysts हैं।
Trends पर भरोसा करने से पहले दो caution। पहला, heavier four d और five d members higher oxidation states favour करते हैं — p-block के inert-pair का बिल्कुल opposite।
दूसरा, reactive relative है। पहली series के ज़्यादातर metals mineral acids में घुल जाते हैं, पर copper comparatively noble है और मना कर देता है, ये बात electrode potentials में फिर आएगी।

board_events.text: A single $4s$ electron is 'donated' so the $3d$ set reaches a half- or fully-filled arrangement.
Half-filled ($d^5$) and fully-filled ($d^{10}$) subshells carry extra stability.

segments.text: With the definition settled, let us write the configurations, and meet the two famous rule-breakers of the three d series.
You would expect the four s to fill neatly before the three d, and mostly it does. But two elements refuse.
First, chromium, atomic number twenty four. Instead of three d four, four s two, it is argon core, three d five, four s one.
Second, copper, atomic number twenty nine. Instead of three d nine, four s two, it is argon core, three d ten, four s one.
The orbital boxes show what happened. In each case one four s electron has been donated inward so the three d set can reach a specially neat arrangement.
For chromium that arrangement is a half-filled d five, one electron in each of the five d orbitals; for copper it is a fully-filled d ten.
The lesson is a theme for the whole chapter: half-filled and fully-filled d-subshells carry extra stability, and elements will rearrange to reach them. We will use this idea again and again.
Definition तय होने के बाद, अब configurations लिखते हैं, और three d series के दो मशहूर rule-breakers से मिलते हैं।
आप expect करोगे कि four s पहले neatly भरे, फिर three d, और ज़्यादातर ऐसा ही होता है। पर दो elements मना कर देते हैं।
पहला, chromium, atomic number twenty four। three d four, four s two के बजाय ये है argon core, three d five, four s one।
दूसरा, copper, atomic number twenty nine। three d nine, four s two के बजाय ये है argon core, three d ten, four s one।
Orbital boxes दिखा रहे हैं क्या हुआ। हर case में एक four s electron अंदर donate हुआ ताकि three d set एक specially neat arrangement तक पहुँच सके।
Chromium के लिए वो arrangement है half-filled d five, पाँचों d orbitals में एक-एक electron; copper के लिए fully-filled d ten।
Lesson पूरे chapter का theme है: half-filled और fully-filled d-subshells में extra stability होती है, और elements उन तक पहुँचने के लिए rearrange करते हैं। ये idea बार-बार काम आएगा।

board_events.text: Radii fall early (rising nuclear charge), then level as $d$-electron repulsion offsets the pull.
$5d$ radii $\approx 4d$ radii — the fingerprint of the lanthanoid contraction.
Ionisation enthalpies rise gently — $d$-shielding keeps removing electrons affordable.

segments.text: Let us now read three trends across the first series left to right, because examiners test all of them.
Start with oxidation state. Up to manganese, the highest stable state equals the total of the n s and n minus one d electrons, which also equals the group number.
The step chart shows the climb: scandium plus three, titanium plus four, vanadium plus five, chromium plus six, manganese plus seven.
After manganese it falls off sharply, because pulling out that many electrons past a half-filled core becomes too costly.
Now size. The radius curve falls steeply at the start as rising nuclear charge pulls the electrons in.
Then it flattens through the middle and even rises slightly toward copper and zinc, because mounting d-electron repulsion offsets the nuclear pull.

Going down a group there is a twist: the five d radii are nearly equal to the four d radii, not larger. That near-equality is the fingerprint of the lanthanoid contraction, which we will explain shortly.

Finally, ionisation enthalpies rise only gently across the series, far more gently than in an s or p period, because each added d-electron shields the next fairly well. That gentle rise is precisely why removing a variable number of d-electrons is affordable, and it underwrites the whole idea of variable oxidation states.
अब पहली series में तीन trends left to right पढ़ते हैं, क्योंकि examiners तीनों पूछते हैं।
Oxidation state से शुरू करो। Manganese तक highest stable state, n s और n minus one d electrons के total के बराबर होता है, जो group number भी है।
Step chart climb दिखा रहा है: scandium plus three, titanium plus four, vanadium plus five, chromium plus six, manganese plus seven।
Manganese के बाद ये sharply गिरता है, क्योंकि half-filled core के आगे इतने electrons निकालना बहुत महँगा हो जाता है।
अब size। Radius curve शुरू में steeply गिरता है क्योंकि बढ़ता nuclear charge electrons को अंदर खींचता है।
फिर बीच में flatten होता है और copper-zinc की तरफ थोड़ा rise भी करता है, क्योंकि बढ़ती d-electron repulsion nuclear pull को offset कर देती है।
Group में नीचे जाने पर twist है: five d radii four d के लगभग बराबर होते हैं, बड़े नहीं। ये near-equality lanthanoid contraction का fingerprint है, जिसे हम जल्द समझाएँगे।

आख़िर में, ionisation enthalpies series भर में सिर्फ gently बढ़ती हैं, s या p period से कहीं धीरे, क्योंकि हर नया d-electron अगले को ठीक-ठाक shield करता है। यही gentle rise variable oxidation states की पूरी idea को possible बनाती है।

board_events.text: Three more properties set by the d-electrons
$E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})$ is mostly negative — these metals displace $\text{H}^{+}$ from dilute acids.
Copper is the noble exception at $E^{\circ}=+0.34\ \text{V}$ — it liberates no hydrogen.

board_events.text: Low states give basic oxides, middle states amphoteric, highest states acidic.
Highest oxide state = group number, up to $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$; acidic ones dissolve in alkali.
Colour comes from $d$–$d$ transitions — an electron jumps between split $d$-levels.
So $d^{0}$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless — no partly filled $d$ to jump within.

segments.text: Three more properties round out the trends, and each one traces straight back to the d-electrons.

First, the standard electrode potential for the M two plus over M couple. It is mostly negative, which means these metals sit above hydrogen and displace protons from dilute acids, liberating hydrogen.
The clean exception is copper, sitting at plus zero point three four volts. Being positive, copper is noble and cannot liberate hydrogen from dilute acid, a fact we will lean on later.
Second, oxides. Look at chromium on the board. The acidity of an oxide climbs with the metal's oxidation state.
Chromium two oxide is basic, chromium three oxide is amphoteric, and chromium six oxide is acidic. The pattern is general: low, middle, high maps to basic, amphoteric, acidic.
The highest oxide state again equals the group number, right up to manganese two oxide seven, and those acidic high-state oxides dissolve in alkali to give oxoanions like chromates and permanganates.

Third, colour. The characteristic colours arise from d to d electronic transitions: an electron absorbs a particular visible wavelength and jumps between energy-split d-orbitals, and your eye sees the complementary colour.
This needs a partly filled d-subshell. That single requirement is exactly why d-zero and d-ten ions are colourless, there are simply no d-electrons to promote.
तीन और properties trends को पूरा करती हैं, और हर एक सीधे d-electrons तक जाती है।
पहला, standard electrode potential, M two plus over M couple के लिए। ये ज़्यादातर negative है, यानी ये metals hydrogen के ऊपर बैठते हैं और dilute acids से protons को displace कर hydrogen छोड़ते हैं।
साफ exception है copper, plus zero point three four volts पर। Positive होने से copper noble है और dilute acid से hydrogen नहीं छोड़ सकता, इस बात पर आगे टिकेंगे।
दूसरा, oxides। Board पर chromium देखो। किसी oxide की acidity metal की oxidation state के साथ बढ़ती है।
Chromium two oxide basic है, chromium three oxide amphoteric, और chromium six oxide acidic। Pattern general है: low, middle, high का मतलब basic, amphoteric, acidic।
Highest oxide state फिर group number के बराबर, manganese two oxide seven तक, और वो acidic high-state oxides alkali में घुलकर oxoanions देते हैं जैसे chromates और permanganates।

तीसरा, colour। Characteristic colours d to d electronic transitions से आते हैं: एक electron एक particular visible wavelength absorb करके split d-orbitals के बीच jump करता है, और आँख complementary colour देखती है।
इसके लिए partly filled d-subshell चाहिए। यही एक requirement बताती है कि d-zero और d-ten ions colourless क्यों हैं, promote करने को d-electrons ही नहीं हैं।

board_events.text: More unpaired d-electrons, stronger metal
High melting points come from strong interatomic metallic bonding.
That bonding strengthens as more unpaired $(n-1)d$ electrons join the $ns$ electron sea.

board_events.text: Count peaks near the middle (around Cr) — the most bonding-available unpaired electrons.
Mn dips: its stable half-filled $3d^5$ core resists donating electrons to bonding.
Zn, Cd, Hg ($d^{10}$) donate nothing — soft, volatile, low-melting; Hg is liquid.

segments.text: Here is a reasoning chain that C B S E loves as a give-reasons question: why do transition metals melt so high, and why does manganese break the trend?
The high melting points come from strong metallic bonding between atoms, a sea of shared electrons holding the lattice tightly.
That bonding gets stronger as more unpaired n minus one d electrons join the n s electrons in the sea. So the key quantity is the count of unpaired, bonding-available d-electrons.
The curve on the board tells the story: a broad hump peaking near the middle of the series, around chromium, where that count is largest.
That maximum near the middle is exactly what the counting predicts, more unpaired electrons, stronger bonds, higher melting point.
Now the famous dip. Manganese has a stable half-filled three d five core; those electrons hold on tightly and resist joining the bonding, so its melting point drops below the trend.

And the end of the row collapses. Zinc, cadmium and mercury are d-ten and contribute no d-electrons to bonding at all, so they are soft, volatile and low-melting. Mercury falls so far it is liquid at room temperature.
ये एक reasoning chain है जो C B S E को give-reasons question के रूप में पसंद है: transition metals इतना high क्यों melt होते हैं, और manganese trend क्यों तोड़ता है?
High melting points atoms के बीच strong metallic bonding से आते हैं, shared electrons का एक sea जो lattice को कसकर पकड़ता है।
ये bonding तब strong होती है जब ज़्यादा unpaired n minus one d electrons, n s electrons के साथ sea में जुड़ें। तो key quantity है unpaired, bonding-available d-electrons की count।
Board का curve कहानी बताता है: series के बीच में एक broad hump, chromium के आस-पास, जहाँ ये count सबसे बड़ी है।
बीच में वो maximum ठीक वैसा है जैसा counting predict करती है, ज़्यादा unpaired electrons, stronger bonds, higher melting point।
अब मशहूर dip। Manganese का stable half-filled three d five core है; वो electrons कसकर पकड़े रहते हैं और bonding में शामिल होने से मना करते हैं, इसलिए इसका melting point trend से नीचे गिर जाता है।

और row का अंत collapse हो जाता है। Zinc, cadmium और mercury d-ten हैं और bonding को कोई d-electron नहीं देते, इसलिए soft, volatile और low-melting हैं। Mercury इतना नीचे गिरता है कि room temperature पर liquid है।

sections.title: Lanthanoid contraction and the catalytic shuttle

board_events.text: Two more chains: contraction and catalysis
Across the $4f$ series each new electron shields the nucleus poorly.
So effective nuclear charge creeps up and radii shrink steadily — the lanthanoid contraction.
Result: $4d\approx 5d$ radii, so Zr $\approx$ Hf and Nb $\approx$ Ta — hard to separate; Os, Ir densest.

board_events.text: A catalyst offers a lower path by switching oxidation states temporarily.
Iron is fully regenerated, so a trace suffices — the defining mark of a catalyst.

segments.text: Two final reasoning chains for this subtopic: where the lanthanoid contraction comes from, and how variable oxidation states power catalysis.
Start with the contraction. As we move across the four f series, each added electron enters an inner four f orbital that shields the nuclear charge very poorly.
Because shielding is poor, the effective nuclear charge creeps up across the series, pulling the electron cloud inward, and the radii shrink steadily. That is the lanthanoid contraction.

The pay-off shows up one row below. The accumulated shrinkage almost exactly cancels the expected size jump, so four d and five d members of a group have nearly identical radii. Zirconium matches hafnium, niobium matches tantalum, which is why those pairs are notoriously hard to separate, and why the five d metals like osmium and iridium are the densest elements known.
Now catalysis. A transition-metal catalyst works by temporarily switching oxidation states to open a lower-energy path.
The classic case is iron speeding up the sluggish iodide-persulphate reaction by shuttling between plus three and plus two.
In the first fast step, iron three plus oxidises iodide to iodine and becomes iron two plus.

Then persulphate re-oxidises the iron back to plus three, so the iron is fully regenerated. A trace is enough, and that regeneration is the defining mark of a catalyst, the same logic behind iron in the Haber process and vanadium five oxide in the Contact process.
इस subtopic के दो आख़िरी reasoning chains: lanthanoid contraction कहाँ से आता है, और variable oxidation states catalysis को कैसे चलाती हैं।
Contraction से शुरू। जैसे-जैसे हम four f series में आगे बढ़ते हैं, हर नया electron एक inner four f orbital में जाता है जो nuclear charge को बहुत poorly shield करता है।
Poor shielding की वजह से effective nuclear charge series भर में creep up करता है, electron cloud को अंदर खींचता है, और radii steadily shrink होते हैं। यही lanthanoid contraction है।

Pay-off एक row नीचे दिखता है। जमा हुई shrinkage expected size jump को लगभग पूरी तरह cancel कर देती है, इसलिए group के four d और five d members के radii लगभग identical होते हैं। Zirconium hafnium से मैच करता है, niobium tantalum से, इसीलिए वो pairs अलग करना बेहद मुश्किल है, और five d metals जैसे osmium और iridium सबसे dense elements हैं।
अब catalysis। एक transition-metal catalyst temporarily oxidation states बदलकर एक lower-energy path खोलता है।
Classic case है iron, जो sluggish iodide-persulphate reaction को plus three और plus two के बीच shuttle करके तेज़ करता है।
पहले fast step में iron three plus, iodide को iodine में oxidise करता है और iron two plus बन जाता है।

फिर persulphate iron को वापस plus three में oxidise कर देता है, तो iron पूरी तरह regenerate हो जाता है। एक trace काफ़ी है, और यही regeneration catalyst की पहचान है, वही logic Haber process में iron और Contact process में vanadium five oxide के पीछे है।

sections.title: Key terms and the five superpowers

board_events.text: The vocabulary that ties it together
Interstitial compound: small atoms (H, C, N, B) fill lattice holes — hard, high-melting, inert.
Alloy: metals with radii within about 15% substitute in the lattice — steels, brass, bronze.
Complex formation: favoured by small size, high charge and vacant $d$-orbitals for ligand pairs.
Disproportionation: one state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

board_events.text: VOCCI — Variable OS, Optical colour, Catalysis, Complexes, Interstitial/alloys.

segments.text: Before the worked examples, lock in four definitions and the master mnemonic, because give-reasons questions reuse this exact vocabulary.

An interstitial compound forms when small atoms, hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen or boron, slip into the vacant holes of a metal lattice. Examples like titanium carbide are hard, high-melting, keep metallic conductivity, and are chemically inert.

An alloy is a blend of metals whose atomic radii lie within about fifteen percent of each other, so one substitutes for the other in the lattice. Transition metals form them readily, think steels, brass which is copper-zinc, and bronze which is copper-tin.
Complex formation is strongly favoured by transition-metal ions because of their small size, high ionic charge, and vacant d-orbitals ready to accept electron pairs from ligands.
Disproportionation is when a single oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
The board shows the textbook case: manganese six splits into manganese seven and manganese four. Watch this reaction, it returns in the very next subtopic on permanganate.
Finally, tie it all together with the wheel. Every power radiates from one centre, the partly filled d-orbitals.
Remember it as V O C C I: variable oxidation states, optical colour, catalysis, complexes, and interstitial or alloy formation. One mnemonic, the whole subtopic.
Worked examples से पहले, चार definitions और master mnemonic पक्का कर लो, क्योंकि give-reasons questions यही vocabulary दोबारा इस्तेमाल करते हैं।

Interstitial compound तब बनता है जब छोटे atoms, hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen या boron, metal lattice के vacant holes में घुस जाते हैं। titanium carbide जैसे examples hard, high-melting होते हैं, metallic conductivity रखते हैं, और chemically inert होते हैं।

Alloy metals का blend है जिनके atomic radii एक-दूसरे के लगभग fifteen percent के अंदर हों, ताकि एक lattice में दूसरे की जगह ले सके। Transition metals आसानी से बनाते हैं, जैसे steels, brass जो copper-zinc है, और bronze जो copper-tin है।
Complex formation transition-metal ions में strongly favoured है, इनके small size, high ionic charge, और vacant d-orbitals की वजह से जो ligands से electron pairs accept करते हैं।
Disproportionation तब है जब एक single oxidation state एक साथ oxidise और reduce हो जाए।
Board textbook case दिखा रहा है: manganese six टूटकर manganese seven और manganese four बनता है। इस reaction को देखो, ये अगले ही subtopic में permanganate पर लौटती है।
आख़िर में, wheel से सब जोड़ो। हर power एक centre से निकलती है, the partly filled d-orbitals।
इसे V O C C I से याद रखो: variable oxidation states, optical colour, catalysis, complexes, और interstitial या alloy formation। एक mnemonic, पूरा subtopic।

Unit: the Bohr Magneton, $1\ \text{BM}=9.274\times10^{-24}\ \text{J T}^{-1}$.

board_events.text: Rule: build the ION's configuration, remove $ns$ first, then count unpaired $d$-electrons.
Memorise 1.73, 2.83, 3.87, 4.90, 5.92 — most numericals collapse onto them.

segments.text: This subtopic has exactly one formula worth carving into memory, so let us give it full attention.
The spin-only magnetic moment, mu sub s, equals the square root of n times n plus two, in Bohr Magnetons.
Here mu is the spin-only moment and n is simply the number of unpaired electrons, nothing more.
The unit is the Bohr Magneton, written B M; one B M equals nine point two seven four times ten to the minus twenty four joules per tesla, since a magnetic moment is a current times an area.

Now the shortcut on the board. Read off the ladder: one unpaired electron gives one point seven three, two gives two point eight three, three gives three point eight seven, four gives four point nine zero, five gives five point nine two.
To use it, always build the ion's configuration, not the atom's, remove the n s electrons first, then count how many d-electrons stay unpaired.

<excited>Here is the exam gift.</excited> Memorise that ladder, one point seven three up to five point nine two, and most magnetic-moment numericals collapse to a one-line lookup instead of re-squaring under a root.
इस subtopic में सिर्फ एक formula है जो याद रखने लायक है, तो इसे पूरा ध्यान देते हैं।
Spin-only magnetic moment, mu sub s, equals square root of n times n plus two, Bohr Magnetons में।
यहाँ mu है spin-only moment और n सिर्फ number of unpaired electrons है, बस इतना।
Unit है Bohr Magneton, लिखते हैं B M; one B M equals nine point two seven four times ten to the minus twenty four joules per tesla, क्योंकि magnetic moment एक current times area है।

अब board पर shortcut। Ladder पढ़ो: one unpaired electron देता है one point seven three, two देता है two point eight three, three देता है three point eight seven, four देता है four point nine zero, five देता है five point nine two।
इसे use करने के लिए हमेशा ion की configuration बनाओ, atom की नहीं, पहले n s electrons हटाओ, फिर गिनो कितने d-electrons unpaired बचे।
<excited>ये रहा exam का gift।</excited> वो ladder याद कर लो, one point seven three से five point nine two तक, और ज़्यादातर magnetic-moment numericals एक-line lookup बन जाते हैं।

Step 2: for $\text{M}^{3+}$ remove the two $4s$ first, then one $3d$.

board_events.text: Step 3: by Hund's rule the two $d$-electrons stay unpaired, so $n=2$.

segments.text: Let us run the magnetic-moment procedure end to end on a clean C B S E-level question. We are given a first-series ion M three plus with atomic number twenty three, and asked for its configuration and spin-only moment.
Step one, identify the element. Atomic number twenty three is vanadium, argon core, three d three, four s two.
Step two, form the ion carefully. To make M three plus we remove three electrons, and the golden rule is to strip the two four s electrons first, then one three d electron.
That leaves vanadium three plus as argon core, three d two. Notice we do not write three d one, four s one; the four s always goes first.
Step three, distribute those two d-electrons. The orbital boxes show Hund's rule at work: they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.
So the number of unpaired electrons, n, is two.
Now substitute. Mu equals the square root of two times two plus two, which is the square root of eight, giving two point eight three Bohr Magnetons. Or simply read it off the ladder for n equals two.
चलो magnetic-moment procedure को एक साफ़ C B S E-level question पर पूरा चलाते हैं। हमें first-series ion M three plus दिया है, atomic number twenty three, और configuration व spin-only moment पूछा है।
Step one, element पहचानो। Atomic number twenty three vanadium है, argon core, three d three, four s two।
Step two, ion ध्यान से बनाओ। M three plus बनाने के लिए तीन electrons हटाओ, और golden rule है पहले दोनों four s electrons निकालो, फिर एक three d।
इससे vanadium three plus बचता है argon core, three d two। ध्यान दो हम three d one, four s one नहीं लिखते; four s हमेशा पहले जाता है।
Step three, उन दो d-electrons को distribute करो। Orbital boxes Hund's rule दिखा रहे हैं: वो parallel spins के साथ अलग orbitals में बैठते हैं।
तो unpaired electrons की संख्या, n, है two।
अब substitute करो। Mu equals square root of two times two plus two, यानी square root of eight, जो देता है two point eight three Bohr Magnetons। या बस n equals two के लिए ladder से पढ़ लो।

board_events.text: Sc$^{3+}=d^{0}$ empty; Ti$^{4+}=d^{0}$ empty — both colourless.
Zn$^{2+}=d^{10}$ full — colourless.
Cu$^{2+}=d^{9}$ partly filled — coloured (blue). The only survivor.
Speed rule: in any 'which is coloured' MCQ, delete every $d^{0}$ and $d^{10}$ on sight.

segments.text: This is a classic N E E T speed trap, and the whole point is to answer it without any calculation. We are asked which of scandium three plus, titanium four plus, copper two plus and zinc two plus is coloured in solution.
Do not compute anything. Just remember the one rule: colour in transition-metal ions comes from d to d transitions, which need a partly filled d-subshell.
So mentally tag each ion as d-zero, d-ten, or in-between, exactly as the board shows.
Scandium three plus is d-zero, empty; titanium four plus is also d-zero, empty. Both are colourless.
Zinc two plus is d-ten, completely full. Also colourless.
That leaves copper two plus, which is d-nine, partly filled. It is coloured, the familiar blue, and it is the only survivor. So the answer is copper two plus.

Bank the speed rule for the exam hall. In any which-is-coloured question, instantly eliminate every d-zero and d-ten ion, because they are always colourless, and only the in-between ion is left standing.

ये एक classic N E E T speed trap है, और पूरा मक़सद है इसे बिना किसी calculation के हल करना। पूछा है scandium three plus, titanium four plus, copper two plus और zinc two plus में से कौन solution में coloured है।
कुछ compute मत करो। बस एक rule याद रखो: transition-metal ions में colour d to d transitions से आता है, जिसके लिए partly filled d-subshell चाहिए।
तो हर ion को mentally d-zero, d-ten, या in-between tag करो, ठीक जैसे board दिखा रहा है।
Scandium three plus d-zero है, empty; titanium four plus भी d-zero है, empty। दोनों colourless।
Zinc two plus d-ten है, पूरी तरह full। ये भी colourless।
बचा copper two plus, जो d-nine है, partly filled। ये coloured है, जाना-पहचाना blue, और यही अकेला survivor है। तो answer है copper two plus।
Exam hall के लिए speed rule याद रखो। किसी भी which-is-coloured question में तुरंत हर d-zero और d-ten ion हटा दो, क्योंकि वो हमेशा colourless होते हैं, और सिर्फ in-between ion बचता है।

The drive to reach $d^{5}$ makes Fe$^{2+}$ oxidise readily to Fe$^{3+}$ in aerated water.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main problem that stitches magnetism to redox stability. An aqueous M two plus ion from the three d series shows a spin-only moment of four point nine zero Bohr Magnetons. Identify the metal, and say which state air oxidation favours.
Step one, run the formula backwards. Four point nine zero squared is twenty four, so n times n plus two equals twenty four, which solves to n equals four unpaired electrons.
Step two, find the configuration. An M two plus ion with four unpaired electrons is three d six, in the high-spin aqueous case.
The orbital boxes show it: five d orbitals, one pair and four singles, giving those four unpaired electrons.
Now work back to the atom. If the two plus ion is three d six, the neutral atom is argon core, three d six, four s two, which is atomic number twenty six, iron.
Step three, link to redox. Iron two plus is three d six. Lose one more electron and you get iron three plus, which is three d five, a half-filled and extra-stable configuration.
That drive to reach the stable half-filled d five is exactly why iron two plus readily oxidises to iron three plus in aerated water. Magnetism gave us the identity; stability gave us the chemistry.

अब एक J E E Main problem जो magnetism को redox stability से जोड़ता है। एक aqueous M two plus ion, three d series का, spin-only moment four point nine zero Bohr Magnetons दिखाता है। Metal पहचानो, और बताओ air oxidation कौन-सी state favour करती है।
Step one, formula को उल्टा चलाओ। Four point nine zero का square twenty four है, तो n times n plus two equals twenty four, जो solve होकर n equals four unpaired electrons देता है।
Step two, configuration ढूँढो। चार unpaired electrons वाला M two plus ion three d six है, high-spin aqueous case में।
Orbital boxes दिखा रहे हैं: पाँच d orbitals, एक pair और चार singles, यानी वो चार unpaired electrons।
अब atom तक वापस जाओ। अगर two plus ion three d six है, तो neutral atom है argon core, three d six, four s two, यानी atomic number twenty six, iron।
Step three, redox से जोड़ो। Iron two plus three d six है। एक और electron खोओ तो iron three plus मिलता है, जो three d five है, एक half-filled और extra-stable configuration।
उस stable half-filled d five तक पहुँचने की drive ही वजह है कि iron two plus aerated water में आसानी से iron three plus में oxidise हो जाता है। Magnetism ने identity दी; stability ने chemistry।

board_events.text: One principle, opposite effects on $\Delta_iH_3$
The deciding quantity is the third ionisation enthalpy $\Delta_iH_3$: $\text{M}^{2+}\rightarrow\text{M}^{3+}$.

board_events.text: Mn$^{2+}=3d^{5}$: removing a third electron breaks the stable half-filled core.
So $\Delta_iH_3(\text{Mn})$ is abnormally large — Mn$^{3+}$ wants to fall back → strong oxidiser.
Fe$^{2+}=3d^{6}$: removing the third electron REACHES the stable $3d^{5}$.
So $\Delta_iH_3(\text{Fe})$ is small — Fe$^{3+}$ forms readily and is stable.

segments.text: Finally, a J E E Advanced reasoning question that shows one principle acting in two opposite directions. Why is manganese three plus a powerful oxidiser, while iron three plus, just one atomic number away, is comparatively stable?
The quantity that decides it is the third ionisation enthalpy, the energy to go from M two plus to M three plus.
The board splits the picture. On one side manganese; on the other iron. The same stable half-filled d five is doing opposite jobs.
Take manganese first. Manganese two plus is three d five, a stable half-filled core. Removing a third electron means breaking that stability.
So the third ionisation enthalpy for manganese is abnormally large. Energetically manganese three plus wants to fall back to manganese two plus, which is exactly why it is a strong oxidising agent.
Now iron. Iron two plus is three d six. Removing the third electron here creates the stable half-filled iron three plus, three d five.

That is energetically favourable, so iron's third ionisation enthalpy is comparatively small, iron three plus forms readily, and it is stable. One principle, the extra stability of three d five, quantitatively reconciles both observations, and it echoes in their reduction potentials too.

आख़िर में, एक J E E Advanced reasoning question जो एक principle को दो opposite directions में दिखाता है। Manganese three plus powerful oxidiser क्यों है, जबकि iron three plus, सिर्फ एक atomic number दूर, comparatively stable है?
इसे तय करने वाली quantity है third ionisation enthalpy, M two plus से M three plus जाने की energy।
Board picture को बाँटता है। एक तरफ manganese; दूसरी तरफ iron। वही stable half-filled d five opposite काम कर रहा है।
पहले manganese। Manganese two plus three d five है, एक stable half-filled core। तीसरा electron हटाना यानी उस stability को तोड़ना।
तो manganese की third ionisation enthalpy abnormally large है। Energetically manganese three plus वापस manganese two plus बनना चाहता है, इसीलिए ये strong oxidising agent है।
अब iron। Iron two plus three d six है। यहाँ तीसरा electron हटाने से stable half-filled iron three plus बनता है, three d five।

ये energetically favourable है, इसलिए iron की third ionisation enthalpy comparatively small है, iron three plus आसानी से बनता है, और stable है। एक principle, three d five की extra stability, दोनों observations को quantitatively समझा देता है, और उनके reduction potentials में भी झलकता है।

board_events.text: Four traps that silently corrupt answers
Trap 1: removing $d$ before $s$. Always strip $ns$ first — Fe$^{2+}$ is $3d^{6}$, never $3d^{4}4s^{2}$.
Trap 2: calling Zn/Cd/Hg transition metals. Test the ion for a partly filled $d$.
Trap 3: assuming every compound is coloured — $d^{0}$ and $d^{10}$ are colourless, diamagnetic.
Trap 4: the heavy-member trend — $4d$, $5d$ favour HIGHER states (Mo, W $\gt$ Cr).

segments.text: Let us close the subtopic with four traps that quietly cost marks, and two pro-tips that buy speed.

Trap one, the most damaging. When forming a cation, always strip the n s electrons first. Iron two plus is three d six, never three d four, four s two. Getting this wrong corrupts every magnetic-moment and colour answer downstream.

Trap two, the exclusions. Do not call zinc, cadmium or mercury transition metals. Test against the ion: is there a partly filled d-subshell in the atom or a common ion? Zinc always fails; copper passes, because copper two plus is d-nine.

Trap three, over-generalising. Not every transition-metal compound is coloured and paramagnetic. The d-zero species like scandium three plus, and the d-ten species like zinc two plus, are colourless and diamagnetic.

Trap four, the heavy-member reversal. In the d-block, the heavier four d and five d members favour higher oxidation states, the opposite of the p-block inert-pair effect. Molybdenum six and tungsten six are more stable than chromium six.
Now the pro-tips. First, the one-second filter on the board: reduce any ion to its d-count; d-zero and d-ten are colourless and diamagnetic, everything in between is coloured and paramagnetic.

Second, to turn a moment back into unpaired electrons, memorise the ladder, one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, five point nine two, rather than re-squaring under the root each time. That is the whole subtopic in your pocket.
Subtopic को चार traps के साथ बंद करते हैं जो चुपचाप marks खाते हैं, और दो pro-tips जो speed देते हैं।

Trap one, सबसे नुक़सानदेह। Cation बनाते समय हमेशा पहले n s electrons निकालो। Iron two plus three d six है, कभी three d four, four s two नहीं। ये ग़लत करने पर आगे का हर magnetic-moment और colour answer बिगड़ जाता है।

Trap two, exclusions। Zinc, cadmium या mercury को transition metals मत कहो। Ion के ख़िलाफ़ test करो: atom या common ion में partly filled d-subshell है क्या? Zinc हमेशा fail; copper pass, क्योंकि copper two plus d-nine है।

Trap three, over-generalise मत करो। हर transition-metal compound coloured और paramagnetic नहीं होता। d-zero species जैसे scandium three plus, और d-ten species जैसे zinc two plus, colourless और diamagnetic हैं।

Trap four, heavy-member reversal। d-block में heavier four d और five d members higher oxidation states favour करते हैं, p-block के inert-pair effect का opposite। Molybdenum six और tungsten six, chromium six से ज़्यादा stable हैं।
अब pro-tips। पहला, board पर one-second filter: किसी भी ion को उसकी d-count में reduce करो; d-zero और d-ten colourless व diamagnetic हैं, बीच का सब coloured व paramagnetic।

दूसरा, किसी moment को वापस unpaired electrons में बदलने के लिए ladder याद करो, one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, five point nine two, हर बार root के नीचे re-square करने के बजाय। यही पूरा subtopic आपकी जेब में।

sections.title: Why they are such aggressive oxidisers

board_events.text: At the top oxidation state, only one way to go: down
In $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ chromium is $+6$; in $\text{KMnO}_4$ manganese is $+7$.
Each equals the group number — the metal's absolute maximum, with nowhere higher to climb.
A metal stuck at its top state is 'maximally hungry' for electrons — the definition of an oxidiser.

board_events.text: Cr($+6$) settles at green Cr($+3$); in acid Mn($+7$) drops to colourless Mn($+2$).
So $\text{KMnO}_4$ is its own indicator: the first excess drop stays purple at the end-point.

segments.text: <curious>Why are these two salts the celebrity oxidising agents of inorganic chemistry?</curious> Every Indian first-aid box has lal dawai, the deep-pink permanganate crystals, and that orange breathalyser tube that turned green was dichromate at work.
Recall a rule from the last subtopic: a transition metal's highest oxidation state usually equals its group number. In potassium dichromate the chromium sits at plus six.
And chromium is in group six, manganese in group seven, so in potassium permanganate the manganese sits at plus seven. Each metal is pinned at its absolute maximum, with no higher state to reach.

A metal stuck at its top state has nowhere to go but down, which makes it maximally hungry for electrons. That hunger, grabbing electrons and getting reduced while oxidising its victim, is exactly what an oxidising agent is.
Picture a strict exam invigilator confiscating phones, the electrons, from students, the reducing agents. As the board shows, the confiscation is visible as a colour change.

Chromium plus six confiscates and settles comfortably at green chromium plus three, so the solution swings orange to green. In acid, manganese plus seven drops all the way to colourless manganese plus two, and the purple simply vanishes.
That vanishing purple is a gift in titrations: permanganate acts as its own indicator. The instant no reductant is left, the very next drop stays purple, marking the end-point without any added dye.

<curious>ये दोनों salts inorganic chemistry के celebrity oxidising agents क्यों हैं?</curious> हर Indian first-aid box में lal dawai होती है, deep-pink permanganate crystals, और वो orange breathalyser tube जो green हुआ वो dichromate था।
पिछले subtopic का rule याद करो: transition metal की highest oxidation state आमतौर पर group number के बराबर होती है। Potassium dichromate में chromium plus six पर है।
Chromium group six में है, manganese group seven में, तो potassium permanganate में manganese plus seven पर बैठा है। हर metal अपने absolute maximum पर pinned है, कोई higher state बची नहीं।

Top state पर अटका metal सिर्फ नीचे जा सकता है, जो इसे electrons के लिए maximally hungry बनाता है। वो hunger, electrons छीनना और ख़ुद reduce होकर victim को oxidise करना, यही oxidising agent की definition है।
एक strict exam invigilator सोचो जो students यानी reducing agents से phones यानी electrons confiscate करता है। जैसे board दिखा रहा है, ये confiscation colour change के रूप में दिखता है।

Chromium plus six confiscate करके green chromium plus three पर आराम से settle होता है, तो solution orange से green होता है। Acid में manganese plus seven पूरा गिरकर colourless manganese plus two बनता है, और purple ग़ायब हो जाता है।
वो ग़ायब होता purple titrations में एक gift है: permanganate ख़ुद अपना indicator है। जिस पल कोई reductant नहीं बचता, अगली ही drop purple रह जाती है, end-point मार्क करती है बिना किसी dye के।

board_events.text: Acidic gains 5, neutral 3, strongly alkaline 1 — ending at Mn$^{2+}$, MnO$_2$, MnO$_4^{2-}$.
Those electron counts 5, 3, 1 are exactly the n-factors used in the equivalent-mass work.

segments.text: There is a deeper subtlety hiding in permanganate chemistry, and it is the single most exam-relevant pattern in this subtopic. How far the manganese falls depends entirely on the medium it reacts in.
The board captures it in one branching picture. Same invigilator, three different rulebooks depending on the room.
In strongly acidic solution, permanganate grabs five electrons and lands at manganese plus two, which is nearly colourless, with water as the other product.
In neutral or faintly alkaline solution it grabs only three electrons and stops at brown manganese dioxide, releasing hydroxide.
In strongly alkaline solution it grabs just one electron and rests at green manganate, manganese plus six.

So read it off as five, three, one: acidic to manganese plus two, neutral to manganese dioxide, alkaline to manganate. As the acid weakens, manganese accepts fewer electrons and stops at a higher oxidation state.
<whisper>Here is the connection that unlocks the numericals.</whisper> Those electron counts, five, three and one, are exactly the n-factors we will feed into the equivalent-mass formula in a moment.
Permanganate chemistry में एक deeper subtlety छिपी है, और ये इस subtopic का सबसे exam-relevant pattern है। Manganese कितना नीचे गिरता है, ये पूरी तरह medium पर निर्भर करता है।
Board इसे एक branching picture में पकड़ता है। वही invigilator, room के हिसाब से तीन अलग rulebooks।
Strongly acidic solution में permanganate पाँच electrons पकड़ता है और manganese plus two पर आता है, जो nearly colourless है, दूसरा product water।
Neutral या faintly alkaline solution में ये सिर्फ तीन electrons पकड़ता है और brown manganese dioxide पर रुकता है, hydroxide छोड़ता है।
Strongly alkaline solution में ये सिर्फ एक electron पकड़ता है और green manganate पर रुकता है, manganese plus six।

तो इसे five, three, one की तरह पढ़ो: acidic में manganese plus two, neutral में manganese dioxide, alkaline में manganate। Acid जितना weak होता है, manganese उतने कम electrons लेता है और higher oxidation state पर रुकता है।
<whisper>ये रही वो connection जो numericals खोल देती है।</whisper> वो electron counts, five, three और one, ठीक वही n-factors हैं जो हम एक पल में equivalent-mass formula में डालेंगे।

board_events.text: Dichromate, Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$, is two such tetrahedra joined at one shared corner oxygen.
The Cr–O–Cr bridge is bent, about $126^{\circ}$ — a favourite one-mark recall.
Manganate MnO$_4^{2-}$ and permanganate MnO$_4^{-}$ are both tetrahedral.
Their $\pi$-bonding comes from oxygen $p$-orbitals overlapping manganese $d$-orbitals.

segments.text: Before the reactions, fix the shapes of the four oxoanions in your head, because a structure question is easy marks and students routinely fumble the bridge.
Start simple. The chromate ion is a single regular tetrahedron: one central chromium with four oxygens at the corners.
The board draws the dichromate ion, and this is the one to get right.
Dichromate is two chromate-type tetrahedra joined together at a single shared corner oxygen, the bridging oxygen sitting between the two chromium centres.

The key detail examiners love: that chromium, oxygen, chromium bridge is not straight, it is bent at about one hundred twenty six degrees. The whole two-chromium unit carries a net charge of two minus.
Now manganese. Both manganate and permanganate are tetrahedral, four oxygens around one manganese, differing only in charge.
In both, the pi-bonding that stiffens the ion arises from overlap of the oxygen p-orbitals with the manganese d-orbitals, the same p to d overlap you will meet again in bonding chapters.
Reactions से पहले, चारों oxoanions के shapes दिमाग़ में fix कर लो, क्योंकि structure question आसान marks है और students अक्सर bridge पर गड़बड़ करते हैं।
Simple से शुरू। Chromate ion एक single regular tetrahedron है: एक central chromium, चार oxygens corners पर।
Board dichromate ion बनाता है, और इसे सही करना ज़रूरी है।
Dichromate दो chromate-type tetrahedra है जो एक single shared corner oxygen पर जुड़े हैं, bridging oxygen दोनों chromium centres के बीच बैठा।
Examiners को पसंद key detail: वो chromium, oxygen, chromium bridge सीधा नहीं है, ये लगभग one hundred twenty six degrees पर bent है। पूरे two-chromium unit पर net charge two minus है।
अब manganese। Manganate और permanganate दोनों tetrahedral हैं, एक manganese के चारों ओर चार oxygens, फ़र्क़ सिर्फ charge का।
दोनों में, ion को stiffen करने वाली pi-bonding oxygen p-orbitals और manganese d-orbitals के overlap से आती है, वही p to d overlap जो bonding chapters में फिर मिलेगा।

<text x="240" y="140" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">L M C T charge transfer</text>
<text x="240" y="205" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle">MnO₄²⁻ is d¹ (paramagnetic); MnO₄⁻ is d⁰ (diamagnetic)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Dichromate orange, chromate yellow, Cr$^{3+}$ green; permanganate purple, manganate green.
Mn$^{2+}$ is nearly colourless; MnO$_2$ is brown.
In MnO$_4^{-}$ Mn is $d^0$ — no $d$-electrons to promote, so the colour is NOT a $d$–$d$ transition.
It comes from a ligand-to-metal charge transfer, L M C T: oxygen $\rightarrow$ manganese.
Same for chromate and dichromate (Cr is $d^0$); MnO$_4^{2-}$ is $d^1$ paramagnetic, MnO$_4^{-}$ is $d^0$ diamagnetic.

segments.text: Colour is where most MCQs on these salts are won or lost, and there is a beautiful subtlety that traps students who over-apply the last subtopic's rule.
First, memorise the palette on the board, because questions hinge on it directly.
Dichromate is orange, chromate is yellow, and reduced chromium three plus is green. On the manganese side, permanganate is purple and manganate is green.
Manganese plus two is so pale it is nearly colourless, and manganese dioxide is brown.

Now the trap. In permanganate, manganese is at plus seven, which is d-zero, it has no d-electrons at all. So its intense purple cannot possibly come from a d to d transition, there is nothing to promote.
Instead the colour arises from a ligand-to-metal charge transfer band, written L M C T, in which an electron shifts from oxygen towards manganese when light is absorbed.

The same is true for chromate and dichromate, since chromium there is also d-zero. And note the magnetism: manganate is d-one, so it is paramagnetic with one unpaired electron, while permanganate is d-zero and therefore diamagnetic.
इन salts पर ज़्यादातर MCQs colour पर जीते या हारे जाते हैं, और यहाँ एक सुंदर subtlety है जो पिछले subtopic का rule over-apply करने वालों को फँसाती है।
पहले board पर palette याद करो, क्योंकि questions सीधे इस पर टिकते हैं।
Dichromate orange है, chromate yellow, और reduced chromium three plus green। Manganese side पर permanganate purple और manganate green।
Manganese plus two इतना pale है कि nearly colourless, और manganese dioxide brown।
अब trap। Permanganate में manganese plus seven पर है, यानी d-zero, इसके पास कोई d-electrons ही नहीं। तो इसका intense purple d to d transition से नहीं आ सकता, promote करने को कुछ है ही नहीं।
बल्कि colour एक ligand-to-metal charge transfer band से आता है, लिखते हैं L M C T, जिसमें light absorb होने पर एक electron oxygen से manganese की तरफ shift होता है।

यही chromate और dichromate के लिए सच है, क्योंकि वहाँ chromium भी d-zero है। और magnetism देखो: manganate d-one है, तो एक unpaired electron के साथ paramagnetic, जबकि permanganate d-zero है इसलिए diamagnetic।

board_events.text: Step 1: oxidative alkali fusion in air; insoluble Fe$_2$O$_3$ is filtered off.
Why KCl? K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ is far less soluble, so it crystallises out while NaCl stays dissolved.

segments.text: Preparation questions are almost guaranteed marks on this subtopic, so let us walk the dichromate manufacture step by step. The starting ore is chromite, iron chromium oxide.
The flow on the board runs ore, to yellow chromate, to orange dichromate, to the potassium salt. Follow it once and the equations write themselves.
Step one, on the board as a full equation: powdered chromite is fused with sodium carbonate in free access of air.
This oxidative alkali fusion gives soluble yellow sodium chromate, and the iron leaves as insoluble iron three oxide, which is simply filtered off to separate it.
Step two, acidify the chromate. Adding acid converts yellow sodium chromate into orange sodium dichromate, the same yellow-to-orange swing we will formalise as an equilibrium shortly.
Step three, convert to the potassium salt by treating with potassium chloride.

And here is the elegant part, a favourite reasoning question. Why potassium chloride? Because potassium dichromate is far less soluble than the deliquescent sodium salt, so on cooling the hot solution the potassium dichromate crystallises out as orange crystals while the sodium chloride stays behind in solution. It is a neat solubility-driven separation.
इस subtopic पर preparation questions लगभग guaranteed marks हैं, तो dichromate manufacture step by step देखते हैं। Starting ore है chromite, iron chromium oxide।
Board पर flow चलता है ore, फिर yellow chromate, फिर orange dichromate, फिर potassium salt। एक बार follow करो तो equations ख़ुद लिख जाते हैं।
Step one, board पर full equation के रूप में: powdered chromite को sodium carbonate के साथ खुली हवा में fuse किया जाता है।
ये oxidative alkali fusion soluble yellow sodium chromate देता है, और iron insoluble iron three oxide के रूप में निकल जाता है, जिसे बस filter करके अलग कर देते हैं।
Step two, chromate को acidify करो। Acid डालने पर yellow sodium chromate, orange sodium dichromate में बदलता है, वही yellow-to-orange swing जिसे हम जल्द equilibrium के रूप में formalise करेंगे।
Step three, potassium chloride से treat करके potassium salt में बदलो।

और ये रहा elegant हिस्सा, एक favourite reasoning question। Potassium chloride क्यों? क्योंकि potassium dichromate, deliquescent sodium salt से कहीं कम soluble है, तो hot solution ठंडा होने पर potassium dichromate orange crystals के रूप में crystallise हो जाता है जबकि sodium chloride solution में रह जाता है। ये एक neat solubility-driven separation है।

board_events.text: Fuse to green manganate, then oxidise to purple

board_events.text: Step 1: alkaline oxidative fusion of pyrolusite gives dark-green manganate, Mn($+6$).
Step 2: oxidise Mn($+6$) to Mn($+7$) — electrolytically, or in the lab by disproportionation.
Mn($+6$) is unstable between $+7$ and $+4$, so it splits one up, one down — textbook disproportionation.

segments.text: Now the permanganate preparation, which pairs neatly with the dichromate one. Here the ore is pyrolusite, manganese dioxide, with manganese starting at plus four.
The board traces the colour journey: manganese dioxide, to dark-green manganate, to purple permanganate.
Step one, on the board: fuse the manganese dioxide with potassium hydroxide and an oxidant such as air or potassium nitrate.
This alkaline oxidative fusion produces the dark-green manganate ion, in which manganese has risen to plus six.

Step two, oxidise that manganese plus six up to plus seven. Commercially this is done by electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution, but in the laboratory the manganate simply disproportionates once the medium turns neutral or acidic.
The board shows the disproportionation: three manganate ions plus acid give two permanganate ions, plus manganese dioxide, plus water.

The reasoning is pure textbook. Manganese plus six is unstable relative to plus seven above it and plus four below it, so a single oxidation state splits into one higher and one lower. That is the very definition of disproportionation we met last subtopic.
अब permanganate preparation, जो dichromate वाली के साथ अच्छी तरह pair होती है। यहाँ ore है pyrolusite, manganese dioxide, manganese plus four से शुरू।
Board colour journey दिखाता है: manganese dioxide, फिर dark-green manganate, फिर purple permanganate।
Step one, board पर: manganese dioxide को potassium hydroxide और एक oxidant जैसे air या potassium nitrate के साथ fuse करो।
ये alkaline oxidative fusion dark-green manganate ion बनाती है, जिसमें manganese plus six तक बढ़ गया है।

Step two, उस manganese plus six को plus seven तक oxidise करो। Commercially ये alkaline solution में electrolytic oxidation से होता है, पर laboratory में medium neutral या acidic होते ही manganate बस disproportionate हो जाता है।
Board disproportionation दिखाता है: तीन manganate ions plus acid देते हैं दो permanganate ions, plus manganese dioxide, plus water।

Reasoning pure textbook है। Manganese plus six, ऊपर plus seven और नीचे plus four के relative unstable है, तो एक single oxidation state एक higher और एक lower में split हो जाता है। यही disproportionation की definition है जो पिछले subtopic में मिली।

sections.title: The chromate to dichromate pH equilibrium

board_events.text: A colour switch with no change in oxidation state
In water the two ions freely interconvert; the acidity alone decides which one dominates.

board_events.caption: Acid shifts right to orange; base shifts left to yellow
board_events.svg:

<text x="240" y="95" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="20" text-anchor="middle">⇌</text>
<text x="240" y="120" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">pH ≈ 4</text>
<rect x="290" y="70" width="150" height="60" fill="#ea580c" stroke="#1e293b"/>
<text x="365" y="95" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff" font-weight="bold">Cr₂O₇²⁻</text>
<text x="365" y="115" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">orange</text>
<text x="200" y="160" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#b00020">add H⁺ →</text>
<text x="285" y="160" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1d4ed8">← add OH⁻</text>
<text x="240" y="188" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">Cr stays +6 throughout — this is NOT a redox change</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Add acid, raise $[\text{H}^{+}]$: equilibrium shifts right to orange dichromate.
Add base: it shifts left to yellow chromate. The two coexist around $\text{pH}\approx 4$.
Chromium stays $+6$ the whole time — this is an acid–base interconversion, NOT a redox reaction.

segments.text: Here is a reaction students constantly misfile as redox, so let us pin it down. In aqueous solution chromate and dichromate interconvert, and the trigger is simply the acidity.
The key framing is that both ions are always present together in water; you are never choosing between two different substances, only shifting the balance by changing how acidic the solution is.
The board gives the equilibrium: two chromate ions plus two protons are in balance with one dichromate ion plus water.
Watch what acidity does to it, shown on the seesaw diagram.
Add acid, that is, raise the hydrogen-ion concentration, and by Le Chatelier the equilibrium shifts to the right, toward orange dichromate.
Add base and it shifts back to the left, toward yellow chromate. In practice the two ions coexist around a p H of about four, a handy laboratory cue.

Now the crucial point that saves you marks. Throughout this whole interconversion, chromium stays at plus six on both sides. No electrons are transferred, so this is an acid-base interconversion, not a redox reaction, and you must never write it with electrons.
ये एक reaction है जिसे students लगातार redox समझ बैठते हैं, तो इसे साफ़ कर लेते हैं। Aqueous solution में chromate और dichromate आपस में बदलते हैं, और trigger सिर्फ acidity है।
मुख्य framing ये है कि दोनों ions water में हमेशा साथ मौजूद रहते हैं; आप दो अलग substances में से चुन नहीं रहे, बस solution कितना acidic है ये बदलकर balance shift कर रहे हैं।
Board equilibrium देता है: दो chromate ions plus दो protons, एक dichromate ion plus water के साथ balance में हैं।
देखो acidity इसके साथ क्या करती है, seesaw diagram पर दिखाया।
Acid डालो, यानी hydrogen-ion concentration बढ़ाओ, और Le Chatelier से equilibrium दाईं तरफ shift होता है, orange dichromate की ओर।
Base डालो तो ये बाईं तरफ लौटता है, yellow chromate की ओर। Practically दोनों ions लगभग p H four के आस-पास coexist करते हैं, एक handy laboratory cue।

अब वो crucial बात जो marks बचाती है। इस पूरे interconversion में chromium दोनों तरफ plus six पर रहता है। कोई electrons transfer नहीं होते, तो ये acid-base interconversion है, redox नहीं, और इसे electrons के साथ कभी मत लिखो।

sections.title: Oxidant strength, standards and the acid rule

board_events.text: Which reagent, and how to acidify it
Permanganate is the stronger oxidant and is its own indicator — convenient for many titrations.

board_events.caption: Strength versus analytical reliability

<line x1="40" y1="45" x2="440" y2="45" stroke="#1e293b"/>
<line x1="240" y1="45" x2="240" y2="195" stroke="#1e293b"/>

<text x="140" y="90" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">E° = +1.51 V (stronger)</text><text x="340" y="90" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">E° = +1.33 V</text><text x="140" y="118" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">self-indicator</text><text x="340" y="118" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">needs indicator</text><text x="140" y="146" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">secondary standard</text><text x="340" y="146" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">primary standard</text><text x="140" y="174" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">decomposes in light</text><text x="340" y="174" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">weighed directly, keeps</text>
<text x="240" y="200" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">acidify with dilute H₂SO₄ — never HCl (Cl⁻ would be oxidised)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Yet dichromate is preferred for accuracy: a primary standard, weighed directly, keeps indefinitely.
Acidify $\text{KMnO}_4$ with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, NEVER HCl — HCl is oxidised, wasting the oxidant.
A favourable $E^{\circ}$ is not a fast rate: permanganate should oxidise water but does so immeasurably slowly.

segments.text: A classic conceptual question asks which of the two oxidants to reach for, and the honest answer is that it depends on what you value.

By raw strength, permanganate wins. On the board, its standard reduction potential is plus one point five one volts against dichromate's plus one point three three, so permanganate is the stronger oxidant of the pair.
And permanganate carries a second convenience: because it is its own indicator, you need no added dye, which suits many routine titrations.
The comparison table lays out the trade-off cleanly, strength on one side, reliability on the other.

Yet for the most accurate work, chemists often reach for dichromate instead. It is a primary standard, it can be weighed directly, and its solutions keep indefinitely, whereas permanganate is light-sensitive, slowly decomposes, and must be standardised first as a secondary standard.

Now a rule you must never break. You acidify permanganate with dilute sulphuric acid, never with hydrochloric acid, because hydrochloric acid is itself oxidisable, permanganate would waste itself turning chloride into chlorine and corrupt any quantitative result.

One more caution mixing up thermodynamics and kinetics. A favourable potential does not guarantee a fast reaction. Permanganate should, on paper, oxidise water, yet it does so immeasurably slowly unless the mixture is warmed or catalysed. Dichromate's lower potential, incidentally, is exactly why it tolerates hydrochloric acid.
एक classic conceptual question पूछता है कि दोनों oxidants में से कौन-सा चुनें, और ईमानदार जवाब है कि ये इस पर निर्भर करता है कि आप किसे value करते हैं।

Raw strength से permanganate जीतता है। Board पर इसका standard reduction potential plus one point five one volts है, dichromate के plus one point three three के मुक़ाबले, तो permanganate दोनों में stronger oxidant है।
और permanganate एक दूसरी convenience भी रखता है: क्योंकि ये ख़ुद अपना indicator है, कोई added dye नहीं चाहिए, जो कई routine titrations के लिए ठीक बैठता है।
Comparison table trade-off साफ़ रखता है, एक तरफ strength, दूसरी तरफ reliability।

फिर भी सबसे accurate काम के लिए chemists अक्सर dichromate चुनते हैं। ये primary standard है, सीधे weigh हो सकता है, और इसके solutions indefinitely रहते हैं, जबकि permanganate light-sensitive है, धीरे decompose होता है, और पहले secondary standard के रूप में standardise करना पड़ता है।

अब एक rule जो कभी नहीं तोड़ना। Permanganate को dilute sulphuric acid से acidify करो, कभी hydrochloric acid से नहीं, क्योंकि hydrochloric acid ख़ुद oxidisable है, permanganate ख़ुद को chloride को chlorine बनाने में बर्बाद कर देगा और quantitative result बिगाड़ देगा।

एक और caution, thermodynamics और kinetics मत मिलाओ। Favourable potential fast reaction की guarantee नहीं है। Permanganate को कागज़ पर water oxidise करना चाहिए, फिर भी ये तब तक immeasurably slowly करता है जब तक mixture गरम या catalyse न हो। Dichromate का lower potential, वैसे, ठीक इसीलिए hydrochloric acid tolerate करता है।

board_events.text: Thermal decomposition, lab prep and chromic anhydride

board_events.caption: Three reactions worth memorising

<text x="30" y="129" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11">2 Mn²⁺ + 5 S₂O₈²⁻ + 8 H₂O → 2 MnO₄⁻ + 10 SO₄²⁻ + 16 H⁺</text>

</svg>

board_events.text: Uses: dichromate — primary standard, chrome tanning, pigments, breath-alcohol test.
Permanganate — organic oxidant, volumetric estimations, bleaching, and lal dawai antiseptic.

segments.text: A short cluster of reactions and uses rounds out the properties, and each one shows up in board papers.
The board groups the three reactions worth memorising.
First, both salts release oxygen on strong heating. Permanganate at around five hundred thirteen kelvin gives potassium manganate, manganese dioxide and oxygen.
Dichromate on heating gives potassium chromate, chromium three oxide and oxygen. Permanganate's ready decomposition, sped up by light, is precisely why it fails as a primary standard.
Second, the laboratory preparation of permanganate on a small scale: a manganese two salt is oxidised by peroxodisulphate all the way up to permanganate, with sulphate as the by-product.
Third, the action of cold concentrated sulphuric acid on dichromate, which precipitates red chromium six oxide, also called chromic anhydride, alongside potassium hydrogensulphate and water.

Finally the uses. Dichromate serves as a volumetric primary standard for estimating iron two, iodides and oxalate, in chrome tanning of leather, in chrome pigments, as a glassware cleaner, and in the classic breath-alcohol test.

Permanganate is an oxidant in preparative organic chemistry, a volumetric reagent for iron two, oxalate and hydrogen peroxide, a bleach for wool, cotton and silk, and of course the household antiseptic and water disinfectant, lal dawai.
Reactions और uses का एक छोटा cluster properties को पूरा करता है, और हर एक board papers में आता है।
Board तीन reactions को group करता है जो memorise करने लायक हैं।
पहला, दोनों salts strong heating पर oxygen छोड़ते हैं। Permanganate लगभग five hundred thirteen kelvin पर potassium manganate, manganese dioxide और oxygen देता है।
Dichromate heating पर potassium chromate, chromium three oxide और oxygen देता है। Permanganate का जल्दी decompose होना, light से तेज़, ठीक इसीलिए ये primary standard के रूप में fail होता है।
दूसरा, छोटे scale पर permanganate की laboratory preparation: एक manganese two salt को peroxodisulphate पूरा oxidise करके permanganate तक ले जाता है, by-product sulphate।
तीसरा, dichromate पर cold concentrated sulphuric acid की action, जो red chromium six oxide precipitate करती है, जिसे chromic anhydride भी कहते हैं, साथ में potassium hydrogensulphate और water।

आख़िर में uses। Dichromate iron two, iodides और oxalate के estimation का volumetric primary standard है, leather की chrome tanning में, chrome pigments में, glassware cleaner के रूप में, और classic breath-alcohol test में।

Permanganate preparative organic chemistry में oxidant है, iron two, oxalate और hydrogen peroxide का volumetric reagent, wool, cotton और silk के लिए bleach, और बेशक household antiseptic व water disinfectant, lal dawai।

board_events.text: Assemble the equation from two half-reactions

board_events.caption: Oxidant half + reductant half, electrons cancel

<text x="240" y="24" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Build any redox equation from two halves</text>
<rect x="20" y="45" width="440" height="34" fill="#fed7aa" stroke="#1e293b"/>
<text x="30" y="67" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11">Oxidant half: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14 H⁺ + 6 e⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 7 H₂O</text>
<rect x="20" y="90" width="440" height="34" fill="#e0e7ff" stroke="#1e293b"/>
<text x="30" y="112" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11">Reductant half (scale so 6 e⁻ cancel): e.g. 6 I⁻ → 3 I₂ + 6 e⁻</text>
<text x="240" y="146" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="18" text-anchor="middle">↓ add</text>

<text x="30" y="180" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11">Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14 H⁺ + 6 I⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 3 I₂ + 7 H₂O</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Acidified dichromate oxidises iodide to $\text{I}_2$, sulphide to S, and tin(II) to tin(IV).
The oxalate titration is autocatalytic: the Mn$^{2+}$ it makes speeds up further oxidation.

segments.text: Finally, the canonical oxidising reactions, and rather than memorising each one whole, learn the method that generates them all.
The board shows the recipe: pick the medium-appropriate metal half-reaction, scale the reductant half-reaction so the electrons cancel, then add the two.
For acidified dichromate the half-reaction is fixed: dichromate plus fourteen protons plus six electrons give two chromium three plus and seven waters.
Feed reductants in and you can write anything: acidified dichromate oxidises iodide to iodine, sulphide to sulphur, and tin two to tin four, each scaled to donate six electrons.
For acidified permanganate, here is the workhorse: two permanganate ions oxidise five oxalate ions in acid, giving manganese two, ten carbon dioxide molecules, and eight waters.
Permanganate also oxidises nitrite to nitrate cleanly, two permanganate to five nitrite in acid, a common titration.

One practical warning that confuses students at the burette. The oxalate titration is autocatalytic: the manganese two it produces accelerates further oxidation, so a warm permanganate-oxalate titration starts sluggishly and then suddenly speeds up. Do not mistake that slow start for a dead reaction.
आख़िर में, canonical oxidising reactions, और हर एक को पूरा रटने के बजाय वो method सीखो जो इन सबको बनाता है।
Board recipe दिखाता है: medium-appropriate metal half-reaction चुनो, reductant half-reaction को scale करो ताकि electrons cancel हों, फिर दोनों जोड़ दो।
Acidified dichromate के लिए half-reaction fixed है: dichromate plus fourteen protons plus six electrons देते हैं दो chromium three plus और सात waters।
Reductants डालो और कुछ भी लिख सकते हो: acidified dichromate iodide को iodine, sulphide को sulphur, और tin two को tin four में oxidise करता है, हर एक छह electrons देने के लिए scaled।
Acidified permanganate के लिए ये रहा workhorse: दो permanganate ions acid में पाँच oxalate ions को oxidise करते हैं, देते हैं manganese two, दस carbon dioxide molecules, और आठ waters।
Permanganate nitrite को nitrate में भी साफ़ oxidise करता है, दो permanganate to पाँच nitrite acid में, एक common titration।

एक practical warning जो burette पर students को confuse करती है। Oxalate titration autocatalytic है: जो manganese two बनता है वो आगे की oxidation तेज़ करता है, तो warm permanganate-oxalate titration धीरे शुरू होकर अचानक तेज़ हो जाता है। उस slow start को dead reaction मत समझो।

board_events.text: The workhorse of every volumetric numerical
$n$ = electrons gained per formula unit — the same counts from the 5–3–1 rule.

board_events.caption: n-factors and equivalent masses

board_events.text: Dichromate in acid: $n=6$, so $294/6=49$.
Permanganate: acid $n=5\Rightarrow 31.6$; neutral $n=3\Rightarrow 52.7$; alkaline $n=1\Rightarrow 158$.
Fix the n-factor FIRST — most JEE volumetric numericals collapse the moment you do.

segments.text: This subtopic has one quantitative tool that J E E leans on constantly, the equivalent mass, so let us make it airtight.
The formula is simple: equivalent mass equals the molar mass divided by the n-factor.
And the n-factor is just the number of electrons gained per formula unit, which are the very same five, three and one counts from the medium rule we drilled earlier.
The board tabulates the standard values you should recognise on sight.
For dichromate in acid the n-factor is six, because two chromiums each drop by three, so the equivalent mass is two hundred ninety four over six, which is forty nine.

For permanganate the n-factor tracks the medium: five in acid gives thirty one point six, three in neutral gives fifty two point seven, and one in strong alkali gives the full molar mass, one hundred fifty eight.

<excited>Here is the exam habit that saves the most time.</excited> Before touching the arithmetic, fix the n-factor first. Once you commit to n equals six for dichromate or the right medium value for permanganate, most J E E volumetric numericals collapse into a single division.
इस subtopic में एक quantitative tool है जिस पर J E E लगातार टिकता है, equivalent mass, तो इसे airtight बना लेते हैं।
Formula simple है: equivalent mass equals molar mass divided by n-factor।
और n-factor बस per formula unit gained electrons की संख्या है, जो वही five, three और one counts हैं medium rule से जो पहले drill किए।
Board वो standard values tabulate करता है जिन्हें देखते ही पहचानना चाहिए।
Acid में dichromate के लिए n-factor six है, क्योंकि दो chromiums हर एक तीन से गिरते हैं, तो equivalent mass है two hundred ninety four over six, यानी forty nine।

Permanganate के लिए n-factor medium follow करता है: acid में five देता है thirty one point six, neutral में three देता है fifty two point seven, और strong alkali में one देता है पूरा molar mass, one hundred fifty eight।

<excited>ये रही exam habit जो सबसे ज़्यादा समय बचाती है।</excited> Arithmetic छूने से पहले n-factor पहले fix करो। जैसे ही dichromate के लिए n equals six या permanganate के लिए सही medium value तय करते हो, ज़्यादातर J E E volumetric numericals एक division में सिमट जाते हैं।

board_events.text: Balance the ionic equation, state the colour change

board_events.caption: Two halves add to the balanced equation

board_events.text: Add the halves — the six electrons cancel exactly.
Colour change: orange dichromate to green Cr$^{3+}$.

segments.text: Let us apply the half-reaction method to the single most common board question on dichromate, its reaction with iron two sulphate in acid.
The board shows the two halves stacking into the answer.
Take the reduction half first, the fixed one for acidified dichromate: dichromate plus fourteen protons plus six electrons give two chromium three plus and seven waters.
Now the oxidation half. Iron two loses one electron to become iron three, so to supply six electrons we scale it by six: six iron two give six iron three plus six electrons.
Add the two halves together and the six electrons on each side cancel exactly, which is the whole point of scaling.
The balanced ionic equation is therefore dichromate plus fourteen protons plus six iron two, giving two chromium three plus, six iron three, and seven waters.
And state the observation explicitly, because it carries a mark: the solution changes from orange, the dichromate, to green, the chromium three plus product.
आधे-reaction method को dichromate पर सबसे common board question पर लगाते हैं, acid में iron two sulphate के साथ इसकी reaction।
Board दोनों halves को answer में stack होते दिखाता है।
पहले reduction half लो, acidified dichromate का fixed वाला: dichromate plus fourteen protons plus six electrons देते हैं दो chromium three plus और सात waters।
अब oxidation half। Iron two एक electron खोकर iron three बनता है, तो छह electrons देने के लिए इसे छह से scale करो: छह iron two देते हैं छह iron three plus छह electrons।
दोनों halves जोड़ो और हर तरफ के छह electrons ठीक-ठीक cancel हो जाते हैं, जो scaling का पूरा मक़सद है।
तो balanced ionic equation है dichromate plus fourteen protons plus छह iron two, देते हुए दो chromium three plus, छह iron three, और सात waters।
और observation साफ़ बताओ, क्योंकि इसका एक mark है: solution orange, यानी dichromate, से green, यानी chromium three plus product, में बदलता है।

board_events.text: Purple KMnO$_4$ added to a NEUTRAL reductant
Do not balance — the keyword 'neutral' is the whole answer.

board_events.caption: Match the medium word to 5-3-1

<text x="230" y="150" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">match the medium word to 5-acid / 3-neutral / 1-base</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Acidic would give Mn$^{2+}$, colourless — the trap for reflexive 'acidic' assumers.
Strongly alkaline would give green manganate, MnO$_4^{2-}$.
Neutral / faintly alkaline $\rightarrow$ brown MnO$_2$ precipitate. That is the answer.
Speed rule: the medium word in the question decides the manganese product every time.

segments.text: This N E E T speed trap tests whether you can read the medium and answer instantly, with no balancing at all. Purple permanganate is added drop-wise to a neutral solution of a reducing agent, and we must name the manganese product and its colour.
Do not balance anything. The single keyword neutral is the entire answer, so scan the five-three-one rule and read it off.
The board lines up the three outcomes so the choice is visual.
Watch the classic distractor. If the medium were acidic, manganese would fall to manganese two, which is colourless, and many students pick that reflexively without reading the word neutral.
At the other extreme, a strongly alkaline medium would give green manganate.
But the question says neutral, or faintly alkaline, and there permanganate stops at brown manganese dioxide, which appears as a brown precipitate. That is the answer.

Bank the speed rule: in these questions the medium word decides the manganese product every single time, so match it, acidic to manganese two, neutral to manganese dioxide, alkaline to manganate, and move on.

ये N E E T speed trap देखता है कि आप medium पढ़कर तुरंत जवाब दे सकते हो या नहीं, बिना किसी balancing के। Purple permanganate एक reducing agent के neutral solution में drop-wise डाला जाता है, और हमें manganese product व उसका colour बताना है।
कुछ balance मत करो। अकेला keyword neutral पूरा answer है, तो five-three-one rule scan करके पढ़ लो।
Board तीनों outcomes line up करता है ताकि choice visual हो।
Classic distractor देखो। अगर medium acidic होता, manganese गिरकर manganese two बनता, जो colourless है, और कई students word neutral पढ़े बिना reflexively वही चुन लेते हैं।
दूसरे extreme पर, strongly alkaline medium green manganate देता।
पर question कहता है neutral, या faintly alkaline, और वहाँ permanganate brown manganese dioxide पर रुकता है, जो brown precipitate के रूप में दिखता है। यही answer है।
Speed rule याद रखो: इन questions में medium word हर बार manganese product तय करता है, तो match करो, acidic to manganese two, neutral to manganese dioxide, alkaline to manganate, और आगे बढ़ो।
