board_events.text: Size: smallest in the $3d$; the $4d$ larger; the $5d$ nearly equal to $4d$.
Higher oxidation states grow more stable down a group — Mo, W more than Cr.
Melting point, density and nobility all rise: Os and Ir are the densest elements.
Headline: the $2$nd and $3$rd series resemble each other far more than either resembles the $1$st.
That resemblance is the direct fingerprint of the lanthanoid contraction.

segments.text: Comparing the three transition series is a standard three-mark question, so let us lay the whole table out and, more importantly, extract the single headline.

The board tabulates the first, second and third series across six properties: size, ionisation enthalpy, stability of high oxidation states, melting point and density, reactivity, and complex or metal-metal bond formation.
Take size first. The three d series is smallest; the four d series is larger, as expected from the extra shell; but the five d series is nearly equal to the four d, not larger.
Higher oxidation states become more stable as you go down a group, so molybdenum six and tungsten six are more stable than chromium six.
Melting point, density and nobility all rise down the group, with osmium and iridium being the densest elements known and platinum and gold the most noble.
Now the headline, and this is the mark. The second and third series resemble each other far more than either resembles the first series.

And the reason ties everything back to the f-block: that resemblance is the direct fingerprint of the lanthanoid contraction, which cancels the expected four-d-to-five-d size increase and leaves the two heavier series almost twins.
तीन transition series की तुलना एक standard three-mark question है, तो पूरी table रख देते हैं और, ज़्यादा ज़रूरी, एक headline निकालते हैं।

Board पहली, दूसरी और तीसरी series को छह properties भर tabulate करता है: size, ionisation enthalpy, high oxidation states की stability, melting point और density, reactivity, और complex या metal-metal bond formation।
पहले size लो। Three d series सबसे छोटी है; four d series बड़ी है, extra shell से उम्मीद के मुताबिक़; पर five d series four d के लगभग बराबर है, बड़ी नहीं।
Higher oxidation states group में नीचे जाते ज़्यादा stable होते हैं, तो molybdenum six और tungsten six chromium six से ज़्यादा stable हैं।
Melting point, density और nobility सब group में नीचे बढ़ते हैं, osmium और iridium सबसे dense ज्ञात elements और platinum व gold सबसे noble।
अब headline, और यही mark है। दूसरी और तीसरी series एक-दूसरे से कहीं ज़्यादा मिलती हैं बजाय इसके कि कोई पहली से मिले।

और वजह सब कुछ f-block से जोड़ती है: वो resemblance lanthanoid contraction का सीधा fingerprint है, जो expected four-d-to-five-d size increase को cancel कर देता है और दोनों heavier series को लगभग twins छोड़ देता है।

board_events.text: Alloy steels — Fe with Cr, Mn, Ni, V, W, Co — are the single most important use.
Catalysts: Fe (Haber), V$_2$O$_5$ (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation of oils to vanaspati).
PdCl$_2$ (Wacker), TiCl$_4$/Al alkyl (Ziegler–Natta), Pt/Pd in catalytic converters.
Photography uses light-sensitive AgBr; K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ and KMnO$_4$ are the volumetric oxidants.
f-block: mischmetall for flints; Ln oxides as phosphors and cracking catalysts; Th, U, Pu as fuels.

segments.text: Applications are pure marks, and the catalyst pairings especially reward precise recall, so let us consolidate them.
The board is a lookup table of process against catalyst, worth committing to memory exactly.
The single most important use of these metals is alloy steels: iron alloyed with chromium, manganese, nickel, vanadium, tungsten and cobalt gives stainless, tool and structural steels.

Now the catalysts, the highest-yield recall. Iron drives the Haber process for ammonia; vanadium pentoxide drives the Contact process for sulphuric acid; nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of oils into vanaspati.

Continuing: palladium chloride runs the Wacker process converting ethene to ethanal; titanium tetrachloride with an aluminium alkyl is the Ziegler-Natta catalyst for polyethene; and platinum and palladium sit in catalytic converters.

Two more families. Photography relies on light-sensitive silver bromide, and the compounds potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate, from the second subtopic, are the workhorse volumetric oxidants.

And the f-block earns its keep too: mischmetall for lighter flints, lanthanoid oxides as television and X-ray phosphors and petroleum-cracking catalysts, and thorium, uranium and plutonium as nuclear fuels.
Applications pure marks हैं, और catalyst pairings ख़ासकर सटीक recall को reward करते हैं, तो इन्हें consolidate कर लेते हैं।
Board process बनाम catalyst की एक lookup table है, ठीक-ठीक याद करने लायक।
इन metals का सबसे ज़रूरी use alloy steels है: iron को chromium, manganese, nickel, vanadium, tungsten और cobalt के साथ मिलाकर stainless, tool और structural steels बनते हैं।

अब catalysts, सबसे high-yield recall। Iron ammonia के लिए Haber process चलाता है; vanadium pentoxide sulphuric acid के लिए Contact process चलाता है; nickel oils के vanaspati में hydrogenation को catalyse करता है।

आगे: palladium chloride Wacker process चलाता है जो ethene को ethanal में बदलता है; titanium tetrachloride एक aluminium alkyl के साथ polyethene के लिए Ziegler-Natta catalyst है; और platinum व palladium catalytic converters में बैठते हैं।
दो और families। Photography light-sensitive silver bromide पर टिकी है, और compounds potassium dichromate व potassium permanganate, दूसरे subtopic से, workhorse volumetric oxidants हैं।

और f-block भी अपनी जगह बनाता है: lighter flints के लिए mischmetall, television और X-ray phosphors व petroleum-cracking catalysts के रूप में lanthanoid oxides, और nuclear fuels के रूप में thorium, uranium और plutonium।

board_events.text: The one idea: partly filled, energetically accessible $(n-1)d$ or $(n-2)f$ orbitals.
They give the $d$-block variable states, colour, magnetism, catalysis and complexes (Sub-01).
They make Cr$^{+6}$ and Mn$^{+7}$ powerful oxidants in K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ and KMnO$_4$ (Sub-02).
Their poor self-shielding drives the lanthanoid and actinoid contractions (Sub-03).
And the stability of $d^5$, $d^0/d^{10}$ (and $f^0/f^7/f^{14}$) governs potentials, colours and states (Sub-04).

segments.text: Before the review, let us step back and see the whole chapter as one idea rather than a list to memorise. This is the capstone synthesis.
The board places a single organising fact at the centre, with all four subtopics radiating from it.
That one fact is this: partly filled, energetically accessible n-minus-one d or n-minus-two f orbitals. Everything in this chapter traces back to it.
Those orbitals give the d-block its variable oxidation states, its colour, its magnetism, its catalysis and its complex formation, the five superpowers of the first subtopic.
They are what make chromium at plus six and manganese at plus seven such powerful oxidants in potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate, the second subtopic.

Their poor self-shielding, one f or d electron shielding another badly, drives the lanthanoid and actinoid contractions that fix f-block size, hydroxide basicity, and the second-versus-third-series resemblance, the third subtopic.

And the special stability of the half-filled d-five, the empty and filled d-zero and d-ten, and the f-zero, f-seven and f-fourteen shells governs the electrode potentials, ion colours and oxidation-state choices we catalogued in this capstone. Master that one idea, what the inner electrons are doing, and almost any question in this chapter can be reasoned out from first principles.
Review से पहले एक क़दम पीछे हटकर पूरे chapter को एक idea की तरह देखें, रटने की list की तरह नहीं। ये capstone synthesis है।
Board एक single organising fact को केंद्र में रखता है, चारों subtopics उससे निकलते हुए।
वो एक fact ये है: partly filled, energetically accessible n-minus-one d या n-minus-two f orbitals। इस chapter का सब कुछ इसी पर लौटता है।
वो orbitals d-block को उसकी variable oxidation states, colour, magnetism, catalysis और complex formation देते हैं, पहले subtopic की पाँच superpowers।
वही chromium को plus six पर और manganese को plus seven पर potassium dichromate और potassium permanganate में इतने powerful oxidants बनाते हैं, दूसरा subtopic।

इनकी poor self-shielding, एक f या d electron दूसरे को बुरी तरह shield करना, lanthanoid और actinoid contractions चलाती है जो f-block size, hydroxide basicity, और दूसरी-बनाम-तीसरी-series resemblance तय करती हैं, तीसरा subtopic।

और half-filled d-five, empty व filled d-zero और d-ten, और f-zero, f-seven व f-fourteen shells की ख़ास stability electrode potentials, ion colours और oxidation-state choices चलाती है जो हमने इस capstone में catalogue किए। उस एक idea में महारत पाओ, कि inner electrons क्या कर रहे हैं, और इस chapter का लगभग कोई भी question first principles से reason किया जा सकता है।

sections.title: Worked example: Cr(II) vs Fe(II) as reducing agents [CBSE]

board_events.text: Which is the better reducing agent?

board_events.caption: Read the couple by the config reached
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 460 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="460" height="180" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="22" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Which is the stronger reducing agent?</text><rect x="30" y="45" width="190" height="90" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#15803d" stroke-width="2"/><text x="125" y="66" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Cr²⁺ (d⁴)</text><text x="125" y="88" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">→ Cr³⁺ (d³, stable)</text><text x="125" y="108" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">E° = −0.41 V</text><text x="125" y="126" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#15803d">strong reducer ✔</text><rect x="240" y="45" width="190" height="90" fill="#e5e7eb" stroke="#1e293b"/><text x="335" y="66" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Fe²⁺ (d⁶)</text><text x="335" y="88" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">→ Fe³⁺ (d⁵, stable)</text><text x="335" y="108" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">E° = +0.77 V</text><text x="335" y="126" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">weaker reducer</text><text x="230" y="160" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">more negative couple → Cr²⁺ is the stronger reducing agent</text></svg>

board_events.text: A reducing agent is itself oxidised — the easier the M$^{2+}\rightarrow$M$^{3+}$ step, the stronger.
Cr$^{2+}$ ($d^4$) $\rightarrow$ Cr$^{3+}$ ($d^3$): reaches the extra-stable half-filled $t_{2g}$ — strongly favoured.
Fe$^{2+}$ ($d^6$) $\rightarrow$ Fe$^{3+}$ ($d^5$): also stable, but the driving force is smaller.
The far more negative couple wins: Cr$^{2+}$ is the stronger reducing agent.

segments.text: Let us apply the configuration-reading method to a classic board question: which is the better reducing agent, chromium two plus or iron two plus?
The board sets the two couples side by side.
Start from the principle. A reducing agent is itself oxidised, so the easier the metal-two-plus to metal-three-plus step is, the stronger the reducing agent.
For chromium: chromium two plus is d-four, and losing an electron gives chromium three plus, which is d-three, the extra-stable half-filled t-two-g configuration. So this step is strongly favoured.
For iron: iron two plus is d-six, and losing an electron gives iron three plus, d-five, which is also stable, but the driving force here is smaller.

The potentials confirm it numerically. Chromium three plus over chromium two plus is minus zero point four one volts, far more negative than iron three plus over iron two plus at plus zero point seven seven.

Since the chromium couple is far more negative, chromium two plus is the stronger reducing agent. State that clearly for the mark, and tie it to the reason: reaching a stable d-three drives the chromium oxidation harder than reaching d-five drives the iron one.
Configuration-reading method को एक classic board question पर लगाते हैं: कौन बेहतर reducing agent है, chromium two plus या iron two plus?
Board दोनों couples side by side रखता है।
Principle से शुरू। Reducing agent ख़ुद oxidise होता है, तो metal-two-plus से metal-three-plus step जितना आसान हो, reducing agent उतना strong।
Chromium के लिए: chromium two plus d-four है, और एक electron खोने पर chromium three plus मिलता है, जो d-three है, extra-stable half-filled t-two-g configuration। तो ये step strongly favoured है।
Iron के लिए: iron two plus d-six है, और एक electron खोने पर iron three plus मिलता है, d-five, जो भी stable है, पर यहाँ driving force छोटा है।

Potentials इसे numerically confirm करते हैं। Chromium three plus over chromium two plus minus zero point four one volts है, iron three plus over iron two plus के plus zero point seven seven से कहीं ज़्यादा negative।

क्योंकि chromium couple कहीं ज़्यादा negative है, chromium two plus stronger reducing agent है। इसे mark के लिए साफ़ बोलो, और वजह से जोड़ो: stable d-three तक पहुँचना chromium oxidation को उससे ज़्यादा ज़ोर से चलाता है जितना d-five तक पहुँचना iron वाली को।

board_events.text: Ti$^{3+}$ is $d^1$, Cu$^{2+}$ is $d^9$, Ni$^{2+}$ is $d^8$ — all partly filled, all coloured.
Sc$^{3+}$ is $d^0$ — empty, no $d$–$d$ transition possible.
Answer: Sc$^{3+}$. Colourless $\Leftrightarrow$ $d^0$ or $d^{10}$ (Sc$^{3+}$, Ti$^{4+}$, Zn$^{2+}$, Cu$^+$).
A one-second filter once the $d$-counts are habit — no calculation at all.

segments.text: This N E E T speed trap is the colour rule applied to the whole three-d row, and it should take one second. Which aqueous ion is colourless, titanium three plus, copper two plus, scandium three plus, or nickel two plus?
The method is to reduce each ion to a simple d-x count and then apply the one-second filter.
The board lays them out so the colourless one jumps out.
Titanium three plus is d-one, copper two plus is d-nine, and nickel two plus is d-eight. All three are partly filled, so all three are coloured.
Scandium three plus is d-zero, an empty d-subshell, so no d-to-d transition is possible.

The answer is therefore scandium three plus. The speed rule to bank: colourless is equivalent to d-zero or d-ten, so scan for scandium three plus, titanium four plus, zinc two plus or copper one plus, and that is always your colourless ion.
Notice, as with the lanthanoid version, you compute nothing. Once the d-counts are automatic, this is a one-second elimination, precisely the pace the exam rewards.

ये N E E T speed trap पूरी three-d row पर लगा colour rule है, और इसे एक second लेना चाहिए। कौन-सा aqueous ion colourless है, titanium three plus, copper two plus, scandium three plus, या nickel two plus?
Method ये है कि हर ion को एक simple d-x count में घटाओ फिर one-second filter लगाओ।
Board इन्हें ऐसे रखता है कि colourless वाला उभरकर आ जाए।
Titanium three plus d-one है, copper two plus d-nine, और nickel two plus d-eight। तीनों partly filled हैं, तो तीनों coloured।
Scandium three plus d-zero है, एक empty d-subshell, तो कोई d-to-d transition संभव नहीं।

इसलिए answer है scandium three plus। Bank करने लायक speed rule: colourless matlab d-zero या d-ten, तो scandium three plus, titanium four plus, zinc two plus या copper one plus scan करो, वही हमेशा आपका colourless ion है।
ध्यान दो, lanthanoid version की तरह, आप कुछ compute नहीं करते। जब d-counts automatic हो जाते हैं, ये one-second elimination है, ठीक वो pace जो exam reward करता है।

sections.title: Worked example: Cu vs Zn and H2 liberation [JEE Main]

board_events.text: Why Zn liberates H$_2$ but Cu does not

board_events.caption: Sign of E(M2+/M) decides it
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 460 185" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="460" height="185" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="230" y="22" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Why Zn releases H₂ but Cu does not</text><rect x="30" y="42" width="190" height="70" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#15803d"/><text x="125" y="64" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Zn: E° = −0.76 V</text><text x="125" y="86" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">negative → reacts</text><text x="125" y="102" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">releases H₂</text><rect x="240" y="42" width="190" height="70" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#b00020"/><text x="335" y="64" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Cu: E° = +0.34 V</text><text x="335" y="86" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">positive → no H₂</text><text x="335" y="102" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">high ΔₖH + ΔᵢH</text><text x="230" y="140" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">Cu: large atomisation + ionisation NOT repaid by hydration</text><text x="230" y="160" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">→ couple is non-spontaneous toward H₂ release</text></svg>

board_events.text: To displace H$_2$, $E^{\circ}(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})$ must be negative.
$E^{\circ}(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn})=-0.76$ V (negative) → Zn reacts, releasing H$_2$.
$E^{\circ}(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu})=+0.34$ V (positive) → Cu does not.
Cu's high $\Delta_a H+\Delta_i H$ are not repaid by hydration, so it prefers to stay the metal.
The energy-term reasoning is the point — the sign of $E^{\circ}$ is just its summary.

segments.text: This J E E Main question asks you to explain, in terms of the governing energy terms, why copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute acid whereas zinc does, even though copper sits in the middle of the row.
The board contrasts the two through the sign of their electrode potential.
The governing rule: for a metal to displace hydrogen, its metal-two-plus over metal potential must be negative.
Zinc two plus over zinc is minus zero point seven six volts, negative, so zinc reacts and releases hydrogen.
Copper two plus over copper is plus zero point three four volts, positive, so copper does not liberate hydrogen at all.

Now the energy explanation the question actually wants. Copper has an exceptionally high enthalpy of atomisation and a high ionisation enthalpy, and these are not sufficiently compensated by its hydration enthalpy. Energetically, copper prefers to remain the metal, so the copper couple is non-spontaneous toward hydrogen release.

The examiner's real target is that energy-term reasoning: the positive sign of the copper potential is just a summary of an unrepaid atomisation and ionisation cost. Answer with the three terms, not merely the sign, to secure full marks.
ये J E E Main question पूछता है कि governing energy terms के हिसाब से समझाओ कि copper dilute acid से hydrogen liberate क्यों नहीं करता जबकि zinc करता है, भले ही copper row के बीच में बैठा है।
Board दोनों को इनके electrode potential के sign के ज़रिए contrast करता है।
Governing rule: किसी metal को hydrogen displace करने के लिए, उसका metal-two-plus over metal potential negative होना चाहिए।
Zinc two plus over zinc minus zero point seven six volts है, negative, तो zinc react करके hydrogen छोड़ता है।
Copper two plus over copper plus zero point three four volts है, positive, तो copper hydrogen बिलकुल liberate नहीं करता।

अब वो energy explanation जो question असल में चाहता है। Copper की enthalpy of atomisation असाधारण रूप से high है और ionisation enthalpy भी high, और ये इसकी hydration enthalpy से पर्याप्त रूप से compensate नहीं होतीं। Energetically, copper metal ही रहना पसंद करता है, तो copper couple hydrogen release की ओर non-spontaneous है।

Examiner का असली target वो energy-term reasoning है: copper potential का positive sign बस एक unrepaid atomisation और ionisation cost का summary है। पूरे marks के लिए तीनों terms से जवाब दो, सिर्फ sign से नहीं।

board_events.text: Cr$^{3+}$ ($d^3$) is extra-stable, so Cr$^{2+}$ gives it up readily — most negative ($-0.41$).
Fe$^{3+}$ ($d^5$) is half-filled-stable, so Fe$^{3+}$ is only a moderate oxidiser ($+0.77$).
Mn$^{3+}$ ($d^4$) is not stable; forming Mn$^{2+}$ reaches the stable $d^5$ → strongly driven ($+1.57$).
Co$^{3+}$/Co$^{2+}$ is highest ($+1.97$), dominated by Co$^{3+}$'s huge hydration enthalpy.
Not monotonic in $Z$ — sculpted by resulting-$d^n$ stability plus hydration of the M$^{3+}$.

segments.text: This J E E Advanced question asks you to account for the full order of the metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus potentials: chromium minus zero point four one, iron plus zero point seven seven, manganese plus one point five seven, cobalt plus one point nine seven. Read each couple by what its three-plus product is.
The board shows the same values as bars, negative through large positive.

Chromium three plus is d-three, extra-stable, so chromium two plus gives up its electron readily. That makes the couple the least favourable toward reduction, the most negative, so chromium two plus is the reducing one.
Iron three plus is d-five, half-filled and stable, so the iron two plus to iron three plus step is favourable and iron three plus is only a moderate oxidiser at plus zero point seven seven.

Manganese three plus is d-four and not specially stable, and forming manganese two plus reaches the very stable d-five, so manganese three plus is strongly driven to reduce, at plus one point five seven.

Cobalt three plus over cobalt two plus is the highest, plus one point nine seven, dominated by the exceptionally large hydration enthalpy of the small, highly charged cobalt three plus ion, which powerfully favours its reduction.

So the synthesis: the trend is not monotonic with atomic number. It is sculpted by the stability of the resulting d-n configuration plus the hydration of the highly charged three-plus ion, the very same half-filled and empty-shell logic that runs through the whole chapter.

ये J E E Advanced question metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus potentials के पूरे order का हिसाब माँगता है: chromium minus zero point four one, iron plus zero point seven seven, manganese plus one point five seven, cobalt plus one point nine seven। हर couple को इसके three-plus product से पढ़ो।
Board वही values bars के रूप में दिखाता है, negative से large positive तक।

Chromium three plus d-three है, extra-stable, तो chromium two plus अपना electron आसानी से दे देता है। इससे couple reduction की ओर सबसे कम favourable, सबसे negative होता है, तो chromium two plus reducing वाला है।
Iron three plus d-five है, half-filled और stable, तो iron two plus से iron three plus step favourable है और iron three plus सिर्फ moderate oxidiser है plus zero point seven seven पर।

Manganese three plus d-four है और ख़ास stable नहीं, और manganese two plus बनाना बहुत stable d-five तक पहुँचता है, तो manganese three plus reduce होने को strongly driven है, plus one point five seven पर।

Cobalt three plus over cobalt two plus सबसे ऊँचा है, plus one point nine seven, छोटे, highly charged cobalt three plus ion की असाधारण रूप से बड़ी hydration enthalpy से dominated, जो इसके reduction को ज़ोरदार favour करती है।

तो synthesis: trend atomic number के साथ monotonic नहीं है। ये बनने वाले d-n configuration की stability और highly charged three-plus ion के hydration से गढ़ा जाता है, वही half-filled और empty-shell logic जो पूरे chapter में चलता है।

sections.subtopic: Capstone Reference: Potentials, Colours, Series and Applications
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Four capstone traps
Trap 1: confusing the couples. M$^{2+}$/M gives reactivity toward acids; M$^{3+}$/M$^{2+}$ gives ion redox behaviour.
Trap 2: reading $E^{\circ}$ signs backwards. Negative M$^{3+}$/M$^{2+}$ $\Rightarrow$ the $+2$ ion is the reducer.
Trap 3: forgetting $d^{10}$ is colourless too — only $d^0$ AND $d^{10}$ are colourless.
Trap 4: mispairing catalysts — Haber-Fe, Contact-V$_2$O$_5$, hydrogenation-Ni, Wacker-PdCl$_2$.
Pro-tip: for any M$^{3+}$/M$^{2+}$ question, read the config — does reduction reach a stable $d^3$/$d^5$?
If yes, the $+3$ ion is a strong oxidiser; if it destroys a stable shell, the $+2$ ion is the reducer.

segments.text: Let us close the capstone, and the chapter's teaching, with four traps and the single reasoning habit that defeats most of them.

Trap one, the most common conceptual mix-up. Keep the two couples apart: the metal-two-plus over metal couple tells you reactivity toward acids, while the metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus couple tells you the oxidising or reducing behaviour of the ions. Do not blend them.

Trap two, a sign error. Read the potentials the right way: a negative metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus value means the plus two ion is the reducing agent, while a large positive value means the plus three ion is the oxidiser.
Trap three, an incomplete colour rule. Do not forget that d-ten is colourless too. Only d-zero and d-ten are colourless; everything in between is coloured.
Trap four, mispairing catalysts, which quietly loses easy marks. Lock in Haber with iron, Contact with vanadium pentoxide, hydrogenation with nickel, and Wacker with palladium chloride.

And the pro-tip that ties the whole capstone together. For any metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus question, do not memorise the number, read the configuration. Ask whether the reduction reaches a stable d-three or d-five.

If it does, the plus three ion is a strong oxidiser, as with manganese three plus falling to d-five. If instead the reduction would destroy a stable shell, then the plus two ion is the reducer, as with chromium two plus climbing to d-three. Reason it out, and the signs fall out automatically, no memorising required.
Capstone को, और chapter की teaching को, चार traps और उस एक reasoning habit के साथ बंद करते हैं जो इनमें से ज़्यादातर को हरा देती है।

Trap one, सबसे common conceptual mix-up। दोनों couples अलग रखो: metal-two-plus over metal couple acids के प्रति reactivity बताता है, जबकि metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus couple ions का oxidising या reducing behaviour बताता है। इन्हें मत मिलाओ।

Trap two, एक sign error। Potentials सही तरीक़े से पढ़ो: negative metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus value मतलब plus two ion reducing agent है, जबकि large positive value मतलब plus three ion oxidiser है।
Trap three, एक अधूरा colour rule। ये मत भूलो कि d-ten भी colourless है। सिर्फ d-zero और d-ten colourless हैं; बीच का सब coloured।
Trap four, catalysts mispair करना, जो चुपचाप आसान marks खो देता है। Lock करो Haber के साथ iron, Contact के साथ vanadium pentoxide, hydrogenation के साथ nickel, और Wacker के साथ palladium chloride।

और वो pro-tip जो पूरे capstone को जोड़ता है। किसी भी metal-three-plus over metal-two-plus question के लिए, number मत रटो, configuration पढ़ो। पूछो कि reduction stable d-three या d-five तक पहुँचता है या नहीं।

अगर हाँ, तो plus three ion strong oxidiser है, जैसे manganese three plus d-five पर गिरता। अगर बजाय इसके reduction एक stable shell तोड़ता है, तो plus two ion reducer है, जैसे chromium two plus d-three पर चढ़ता। Reason करो, और signs अपने आप निकल आते हैं, कुछ रटने की ज़रूरत नहीं।

board_events.text: Every formula of the chapter in one place

board_events.caption: Key electrode potentials to carry
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 470 210" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="470" height="210" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="235" y="20" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">Key E° values to carry</text><rect x="20" y="35" width="430" height="46" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1e293b"/><text x="30" y="53" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">M²⁺/M: mostly −ve (displace H₂); Cu +0.34 V is the lone +ve (noble)</text><text x="30" y="71" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">Mn, Zn extra-negative (stable d⁵, d¹⁰)</text><rect x="20" y="88" width="430" height="60" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#1e293b"/><text x="30" y="106" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">M³⁺/M²⁺: Cr −0.41 (Cr²⁺ reducing), Fe +0.77 (mild),</text><text x="30" y="124" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">Mn +1.57, Co +1.97 (strong oxidisers) — via reaching/abandoning d³/d⁵</text><text x="30" y="142" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">Ln³⁺/Ln ≈ −2.2 to −2.4 V (strong reducers)</text><rect x="20" y="155" width="430" height="42" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#1e293b"/><text x="30" y="173" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">μₛ = √n(n+2) BM (d-block); μ = g√J(J+1) BM (lanthanoids)</text><text x="30" y="191" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="10">Eq. mass = M/n: K₂Cr₂O₇ 6→49; KMnO₄ 5/3/1→31.6/52.7/158</text></svg>

board_events.text: Use spin-only for the $d$-block; switch to the $J$-formula for the lanthanoids.

segments.text: Now the chapter review, in two parts. First, every formula collected in one place, so revision is a single glance.
The magnetic workhorse: the spin-only moment, mu-s equals the square root of n times n-plus-two, in Bohr magnetons, valid for the d-block.

Memorise its ladder rather than re-squaring under the root: for one, two, three, four and five unpaired electrons, the moments are one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, and five point nine two.
For the lanthanoids the spin-only formula fails, and the moment follows mu equals g times the square root of J times J-plus-one, the total-angular-momentum expression.

From the dichromate and permanganate subtopic: equivalent mass equals molar mass over the n-factor. Potassium dichromate has an n-factor of six, giving forty nine; potassium permanganate is five, three or one by medium.
The board card collects the key electrode potentials worth carrying into the exam, the metal-two-plus, the metal-three-plus and the lanthanoid couples.
And the oxidation-state rule from the very first subtopic: the maximum oxidation state equals the group number up to manganese, scandium plus three through manganese plus seven.
One habit to remember across all of this: use the spin-only formula for the d-block, but switch to the J-based formula the moment you are dealing with a lanthanoid.
अब chapter review, दो हिस्सों में। पहले, हर formula एक जगह इकट्ठा, ताकि revision एक नज़र में हो जाए।
Magnetic workhorse: spin-only moment, mu-s equals square root of n times n-plus-two, Bohr magnetons में, d-block के लिए valid।

Root के नीचे बार-बार square करने के बजाय इसका ladder याद करो: एक, दो, तीन, चार और पाँच unpaired electrons के लिए, moments हैं one point seven three, two point eight three, three point eight seven, four point nine zero, और five point nine two।
Lanthanoids के लिए spin-only formula fail होता है, और moment follow करता है mu equals g times square root of J times J-plus-one, total-angular-momentum expression।

Dichromate और permanganate subtopic से: equivalent mass equals molar mass over n-factor। Potassium dichromate का n-factor six है, जो forty nine देता है; potassium permanganate medium के हिसाब से five, three या one।
Board card exam में ले जाने लायक key electrode potentials इकट्ठा करता है, metal-two-plus, metal-three-plus और lanthanoid couples।
और बिलकुल पहले subtopic से oxidation-state rule: maximum oxidation state manganese तक group number के बराबर, scandium plus three से manganese plus seven तक।
इस सब में एक habit याद रखो: d-block के लिए spin-only formula use करो, पर जैसे ही किसी lanthanoid से निपट रहे हो, J-based formula पर switch कर जाओ।

board_events.text: One-screen recall for the whole chapter
Sub-01: transition element = incomplete $(n-1)d$ in atom or ion; VOCCI powers; Zn, Cd, Hg excluded; Cr, Cu anomalies.
Colour/magnetism need a partly filled $d$; $d^0$, $d^{10}$ colourless. Lanthanoid contraction $\Rightarrow$ Zr $\approx$ Hf.
Sub-02: dichromate/permanganate prep; structures (Cr–O–Cr $\approx126^\circ$); 5–3–1 rule; colours are LMCT; acidify with dil. H$_2$SO$_4$.
Sub-03: $f$-config $(n-2)f^{1-14}$; $+3$ dominant; contraction from poor $4f$ shielding; $\mu=g\sqrt{J(J+1)}$; La, Ac are $d$-block.
Sub-04: $E^{\circ}$ set by $\Delta_a H+\Delta_i H+\Delta_{hyd}H$; Cr$^{2+}$ reducing, Mn$^{3+}$/Co$^{3+}$ oxidising; $2$nd $\approx 3$rd series.

board_events.text: Catalysts: Haber-Fe, Contact-V$_2$O$_5$, hydrogenation-Ni, Wacker-PdCl$_2$, Ziegler–Natta-Ti, photography-AgBr.

segments.text: Second, the whole-chapter cheat sheet, one screen that consolidates all four subtopics for the night before the exam.

From subtopic one: a transition element has an incomplete n-minus-one d subshell in its atom or a common ion; its five powers spell V O C C I; zinc, cadmium and mercury are excluded; and chromium and copper carry the half- and fully-filled anomalies.

Still subtopic one: colour and magnetism need a partly filled d-subshell, so d-zero and d-ten are colourless and diamagnetic, and the lanthanoid contraction makes zirconium and hafnium nearly identical.

From subtopic two: know the dichromate and permanganate preparations, the structures with the roughly one hundred twenty six degree chromium-oxygen-chromium bridge, the five-three-one medium rule, the fact that the colours are charge-transfer not d-to-d, and that you acidify with dilute sulphuric acid.

From subtopic three: the f-block configuration, plus three dominant, the contraction from poor four f shielding, the J-based magnetic formula, and the reminder that lanthanum and actinium are actually d-block.

From subtopic four: the electrode potential is set by atomisation plus ionisation plus hydration energies; chromium two plus is reducing while manganese and cobalt three plus are oxidising; and the second and third series resemble each other.
The board card gathers the master mnemonics: V O C C I, LA-GD-LU colourless and diamagnetic, and the five-three-one rule.

And finally lock the catalyst pairings, the reliable exam earners: Haber with iron, Contact with vanadium pentoxide, hydrogenation with nickel, Wacker with palladium chloride, Ziegler-Natta with titanium, and photography with silver bromide. That is the entire chapter on a single screen.
दूसरा, whole-chapter cheat sheet, एक screen जो exam से पहली रात के लिए चारों subtopics consolidate करती है।

Subtopic one से: transition element के atom या common ion में incomplete n-minus-one d subshell होती है; इसकी पाँच powers V O C C I बनाती हैं; zinc, cadmium और mercury excluded हैं; और chromium व copper half- और fully-filled anomalies रखते हैं।
अब भी subtopic one: colour और magnetism को partly filled d-subshell चाहिए, तो d-zero और d-ten colourless व diamagnetic हैं, और lanthanoid contraction zirconium व hafnium को लगभग एक जैसा बना देता है।

Subtopic two से: dichromate और permanganate की preparations जानो, लगभग one hundred twenty six degree वाले chromium-oxygen-chromium bridge के साथ structures, five-three-one medium rule, ये तथ्य कि colours charge-transfer हैं d-to-d नहीं, और ये कि आप dilute sulphuric acid से acidify करते हो।
Subtopic three से: f-block configuration, plus three dominant, poor four f shielding से contraction, J-based magnetic formula, और ये याद कि lanthanum और actinium असल में d-block हैं।

Subtopic four से: electrode potential atomisation plus ionisation plus hydration energies से तय होता है; chromium two plus reducing है जबकि manganese और cobalt three plus oxidising; और दूसरी व तीसरी series एक-दूसरे से मिलती हैं।
Board card master mnemonics इकट्ठा करता है: V O C C I, LA-GD-LU colourless और diamagnetic, और five-three-one rule।

और आख़िर में catalyst pairings lock करो, भरोसेमंद exam earners: Haber के साथ iron, Contact के साथ vanadium pentoxide, hydrogenation के साथ nickel, Wacker के साथ palladium chloride, Ziegler-Natta के साथ titanium, और photography के साथ silver bromide। यही पूरा chapter एक single screen पर है।
